subtopic: GUILT BY ASSOCIATION
GUILT BY ASSOCIATION
speechtext: In arriving at their recommendations or decisions in security matters affecting individual government employees, do the security panel and/or the security officers of the various government departments and agencies concerned reject any conclusion based on the principle of guilt by association?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: GUILT BY ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
In reaching a decision as to whether a person should be given access to secret information, there is no question of guilt or innocence. The Prime Minister stated in this connection in the House of Commons on December 3, 1951:
The question at issue is not guilt or innocence of some particular charge. The sole question is whether a certain person can or cannot be entrusted with secret defence material. It would give a completely false atmosphere to the matter if it were assumed that reliability can somehow be put beyond doubt by meeting formal charges-or indeed, that reliability cannot be brought into doubt except on the basis of formal charges. Assessment of character may be the only consideration in some instances. That is not a matter of charges, or of trial or of proof. It is a matter of judgment.
These words were spoken by the Prime Minister in referring to security measures in industries engaged in defence production. They apply with equal force in the public service. Because a person is known to associate with communists does not establish that that person is a communist, nor is that assumed by those in charge of departments. However, in determining whether a person
is or is not suitable for employment in a particular job, a review is made not only of that person's professional qualifications and character but also, where access to secrets is involved, of all the available information bearing upon his reliability and the degree of confidence in which he can be held. If such a review establishes a history of communist associations, it is not assumed that that person is or is not a communist, but it may be decided that there is too much risk involved in allowing a person with such a background to have access to important secret information.
Because it is important to prevent any implication of guilt from attaching to these cases, such transfers and dismissals are dealt with in the same way as other transfers and dismissals, which is only proper since they are all subject essentially to the same criterion: does a given person possess all the qualifications required to fill a given position satisfactorily. The concept of guilt or innocence has no place in this process. The government, as an employer, is not a tribunal nor does it dictate to individuals what they must or must not think or with whom they may or may not associate; but, like any other employer, the government makes every effort to ensure that its employees are properly qualified for the work they have to do-and such qualifications must in some cases include a high standard of reliability.

subtopic: COMMUNICATION TO INDIVIDUAL
COMMUNICATION TO INDIVIDUAL
speechtext: When a decision has been arrived at to release or transfer a government employee for security reasons, does the individual concerned in each case have an opportunity of learning the nature of the allegations or suspicions against him before being transferred or dismissed?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: COMMUNICATION TO INDIVIDUAL
speechtext:
Under normal circumstances the information obtained about a person as a result of a security screening-and any consequent doubts as to the advisability of allowing him access to his country's secrets-are not discussed with a person who, as a result, may be subject to transfer or dismissal. There are cases where the circumstances do permit this to be done. Where a useful purpose could be served, and where security considerations permit, it is done, and an exception is made to normal practice.
The main security considerations necessitating this procedure were given in December, 1951, by the Prime Minister when he spoke in the House of Commons about a security case in defence industry. He said: "There is a further consideration of an entirely different order that is also relevant. It is that hearings could and probably would compromise our general security precautions. Some of the people about whose access to secret material we have to be most concerned operate in the interests of an organization that is skilfully and tightly bound together. This organization acts with a ruthlessness and a readiness to sacrifice its own followers, which we find it almost impossible to appreciate. It is only
*See also page 3290.

by careful, long continued and patient work that means have been established by our police forces of getting information about the operations of this organization. The organization would be more than ready to precipitate hearings involving their own followers, even if it meant the personal ruin of those individuals, if the hearings would lay bare the sources of information that the police have established. If hearings were held, the information as to the background or other considerations causing doubt about an individual would have to be revealed. I do not see how a "hearing" could be regarded as serving any purpose if they were not. More than that, it would be argued that the validity of such information or the grounds for doubt could not be assessed nor could any "charges" be properly refuted unless the kind and sources of information were disclosed, the informants questioned, and so forth. If that were done in even two or three instances, they might be sufficient to nullify, in very short order, such security defences as we have been able to build up after years of painstaking effort. The well-organized opponents of our way of life would be more than ready to sacrifice a good many of their supporters to gain the kind of information that hearings would inevitably reveal."
It follows logically that doubts or suspicions of a person's fitness to know his country's secrets cannot be conveyed to him if, in the public interest, the information which gives rise to those doubts must be withheld. There are cases where, for instance, human weaknesses are the cause for doubt of a person's reliability and in a number of these cases neither the information nor the source of the information may need protection. But in many such cases telling a person about these weaknesses will neither correct them nor remove the doubts which they cause. In the few cases where a purpose might be served and where it could be done safely, security officials are prepared to discuss the matter with the individual in question. But these few individual cases could not justify the application of such a procedure to security decisions in general.
A person who is denied access to secret information has been so treated because in the careful and considered opinion of reasonable men there is doubt as to his reliability. This is a matter of judgment. The Prime Minister spoke of this in his speech in December, 1951, and what he said with regard to defence industry then applies equally to the public service. He said on that occasion: "... we are not in the realm of what have
Orders for Returns
come to be called "human rights" and "fundamental freedoms". There is no human right or fundamental freedom involved. No person has a right of access to secret defence items and no man's freedom is infringed when he is denied such access".
The fact that under our present security system a person may have no knowledge of the reasons why he has been dismissed from or transferred within the public service as a result of a security screening places a very grave and unpleasant responsibility upon the government. The Prime Minister expressed the government's views about it in this way: This means, of course, that the responsibility of the government is the greater to see that every case is carefully assessed and that no decisions as to the reliability of an individual are lightly taken. They are not lightly taken. Moreover, the cases can always be re-examined and the government will have no reluctance about reversing an original decision if further review suggests that it can safely be reversed. This whole matter is, however, distorted and seen in a false light, if it is confused with loyalty and thought of in terms of specific, provable or disprovable charges. You can doubt the reliability of a man for the security of some vital defence matter without considering him to be disloyal. You can continue to doubt no matter how much he argues or protests. The problem that is thrust on the government of assessing the reliability of employees in defence industries, and occasionally of deciding in some cases that reliability is uncertain, is not a pleasant one. In the present state of things it is, however, an unavoidable one. It is the government itself which is and must be answerable for the security of our defence secrets. The government is, however, fully aware of the importance of ensuring in so far as possible that no injury is done to any individual through the decisions that must be taken. Security procedures are constantly under review and if they can be improved, the government will always be ready to make the improvements and will always welcome and seriously consider constructive suggestions to that end.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: RESEARCH INTO RELATION BETWEEN SMOKING AND LUNG CANCER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of news reports over the week end, will the minister make a further statement in reply to my question of about a month ago as to what the federal government is prepared to do in the matter of research into the relation between cigarette smoking and lung cancer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: RESEARCH INTO RELATION BETWEEN SMOKING AND LUNG CANCER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when my hon. friend asked this question a few weeks ago I deliberately refrained from making a statement at that time because of the great importance of this subject. As the house knows, the Canadian cancer institute is the agency in Canada through which cancer research is directed, and through which moneys provided by the federal government in the field of cancer research are allocated. The Canadian cancer institute came into being as the result of an idea proposed by my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), then minister of national health and welfare.
A few weeks ago the officers of my department reviewed with the institute those research projects relating directly or indirectly to cancer of the lung, with special reference to the effects of tobacco and its products.
More recently I conferred with the director and certain officers of the institute regarding this matter. A liaison has been effected with research groups in the United States and in the United Kingdom through Dr. Hartcroft of the department of medical research of the University of Toronto who attended a meeting for this purpose a few days ago in the United States. Following the discussions I had with these officials of the cancer institute, I took occasion to suggest that the tobacco industry might be disposed to provide unconditional grants in addition to those provided by federal and provincial governments for research in lung cancer.
This suggestion has been unreservedly accepted by the industry and the president of the national cancer institute will announce some time today that the institute has received a donation of $100,000 from the Canadian tobacco industry for the support of such research. This fund will be administered at the discretion of the board of directors of the institute which, with the assistance


of their research advisers, is preparing an appropriate plan to encourage further investigation into this form of cancer.
Any grants made from this fund, or from the fund through which federal assistance has been given, will come under the same regulations as any grant in aid of research awarded by the national cancer institute of Canada. It is deemed desirable that I should add that the research program of the national cancer institute embraces a number of projects relating directly or indirectly to cancer of the lung. In addition to certain projects now under way new projects are under consideration at the moment specifically related to the effects of tobacco and its products on the lung and air passages. The statistical officer of the institute has been working on the problem of lung cancer for some time. He has the full co-operation and assistance of the vital statistics branch of the dominion bureau of statistics and of the principal treatment centres of Canada. He has already been of assistance to the department's Indian health services and is working closely with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
So far the clinical and statistical approach to the investigation of cancer is considered to be important. Possibly the largest group of people on whom there are very carefully kept records is the veterans group coming within the field of special interest of my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe). Officers of my department and of the Department of Veterans Affairs have been in consultation regarding cancer in general but more especially primary cancer of the lung. It is agreed by the experts that every effort should be made to derive all the information possible on this subject from the Department of Veterans Affairs records. The records of deaths from cancer to date are being searched for any indication which might help solve some of these problems. Furthermore, the system of recording will be reviewed for the purpose of ensuring that future compilations of statistics will include the necessary data on smoking habits.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. 102, to promote the construction of new houses, the

National Housing Act
repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and building conditions-Mr. Winters-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 36-Federal-provincial projects.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: When the committee rose at its previous sitting, we were discussing clause 36. Shall the clause carry?

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the views expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South last Friday just prior to the time of adjournment. Like the hon. member, I believe that this clause contains some valuable features of Bill 102. As hon. members know, clause 36 reproduces section 35 of the present act. I believe that section has great possibilities. In order to illustrate, I should like to show what has been done at St. John's, Newfoundland, under section 35 of the present act. I turn to pages 28 and 29 of the minutes of the committee on banking and commerce, table "A". There I find that out of a total of 1,712 federal-provincial projects of land assembly completed throughout the whole of Canada in the four years since the inception of the scheme, no fewer than 594 have been completed at St. John's, Newfoundland. That is more than one-third of the total for the whole country. At the same place in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the banking and commerce committee we find that out of a total of 1,832 federal-provincial low rental housing units completed in the whole of Canada during the same four-year period, no fewer than 392 have been completed at St. John's, Newfoundland, more than 20 per cent of the total for the entire country.
The population of St. John's is a good deal less than one per cent of the aggregate population of all the incorporated cities, towns and villages in Canada. Four hundred federal-provincial low rental housing units have been completed in four years at St. John's, Newfoundland, and if a similar proportionate total had been achieved in the other municipalities 40,000 new low rental housing units would have been created under section 35 in four years. That, I submit, would be a not inconsiderable addition to the housing accommodation for those in low income brackets throughout this country.
There are two further points in connection with the experience in St. John's. First of all, I should like to point out that the scheme there has worked out very well. We have the testimony of Mr. Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for that. I turn now to page 124 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence

of the banking and commerce committee where Mr. Mansur describes the scheme at St. John's as highly successful and says:
I believe that the experience in St. John's has been excellent and it has fulfilled our highest expectations.
The second point is that, so far as the experience of St. John's at any rate is concerned, there need be no conflict between the construction of low rental housing and the expansion of home ownership and of economic rental housing. There has been an addition of at least one-third to the total housing units in St. John's over the past ten years and that, I submit, is a rate of growth little short of phenomenal in a city so venerable as St. John's, for ten years is but a brief period in the history of that city. Therefore may I say that I believe clause 36 of the bill provides a basis for a most fruitful partnership between federal, provincial and municipal authorities, and I trust that the municipalities and provinces throughout Canada will take full advantage of the generous offer of 75 per cent participation made by the federal government through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under this plan. We can see what can be done, and I hope that it will be done in the future.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very
glad that the hon. member for St. John's East has placed on record his tribute as to what can be done in the matter of building low rental housing under the provisions of section 35 of the act as it now stands or clause 36 of the bill now before us. I must point out, however, that there are one or two shortcomings so far as this part of the legislation is concerned. In the main the difficulty is that it is possible for a provincial government which is not prepared to accept its full responsibility under this clause to shelve a part of that responsibility by trying to pass it on to a local municipality. When that happens, as it happened in my own city of Winnipeg last year, you come up against a very difficult situation. In Manitoba, as the minister and others know, the provincial government refused to put up the 25 per cent of the cost of a federal-provincial project for my city but contended rather that half of the provincial portion would have to be put up by the city of Winnipeg.
That made it necessary for a bylaw to be placed on the ballot at the last civic election, and according to the city charter that bylaw could be voted upon only by property holders in the city of Winnipeg. To the credit of the people of Winnipeg, there was a very large vote in favour of the bylaw but by no

means sufficient to carry it. When one realizes that the only people allowed to vote on the question were those who already owned property one realizes the significance of a fairly sizeable vote. But the plain fact of the matter is that if you have a provision in the act making it possible for a portion of the cost of a low rental housing project to be levied against existing real property in the form of a real estate tax you run up against a very real barrier.
In my view a provision such as this will only work if the provincial government accepts its share of the responsibility as set out in the act. If you have provincial governments that feel they cannot put up their 25 per cent, or that simply refuse to do so, that raises the question whether the federal government's proportion should not be increased. I believe that it should. I would say that you could separate the two elements referred to in subclause 2 of clause 36, namely, the capital cost and the profits or losses. I would say it is perfectly all right to expect a province to bear 25 per cent of the losses on any such project and that it is financially possible for a province to do that, but it is a different story for a province to find the amount of money involved in 25 per cent of the capital cost.
It looks very nice on paper. It looks as though the federal government is being generous in offering to put up 75 per cent as against 25 per cent on the part of a province, but anyone who thinks about it at all knows that it is easier for the federal government to find the money necessary for its 75 per cent than it is for the provinces to find the money necessary for the 25 per cent. In my view, as long as it is possible for a province such as Manitoba to crawl out from under its share of the burden and try to pass it on to municipalities, the only way a clause such as 36 will work is for the federal government to bear a larger portion of the capital cost. I hope that even yet we may get consideration by the government of that aspect of the clause.
I want to say a word now in reply to something said on Friday night just before we adjourned by the hon. member for Vancouver South. He rose and threw out a statement the like of which he might get away with in his newspaper column but which he can hardly expect to get away with in the house. He said, as recorded at page 2741 of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, we have heard over and over again in this committee of the whole the contention that nothing has been done under this act for people with incomes of less than $3,800. That, of course, Is absolute nonsense, because one of the
National Housing Act
most important clauses in this bill has been carried over from the old act, and it provides very large sums of money indeed for the financing of low rental housing projects to be carried out between the federal government and the various provinces.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver South knows-if he did not realize it when he made that statement he should look back into Hansard and read it now-that those of us who were talking about the failure of this act to be of assistance to those whose incomes were less than $3,800 a year pointed out very clearly that the act does not make possible home ownership for people with incomes of less than that figure. It is true that there is a possibility, if the other levels of government participate, for some assistance to be rendered to people with low incomes under clause 36 of the bill, which has to do with low rental projects. He knows that what we were saying is not nonsense, as he termed it the other night, but the absolute truth, namely, so long as you have that $3,800 cut off point on housing loans, people with incomes less than that figure cannot get loans under this act for the purpose of owning their own homes.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is still an important matter with which this bill fails to deal. I was interested in reading only this morning an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune from my own city which points out that with wages being what they are, this bill is still of no help to the great majority of people so far as home ownership is concerned. We now know that, with the bill as it now stands, one has to have about $76 per week in order to obtain a loan for a $10,000 home, or $90 per week to obtain a loan for a $12,000 home. Since the average weekly wage in the city of Winnipeg, according to recent statistics, is only $52.51 per week, one readily sees how this bill will fail to help the great majority of the workers in my city to obtain a home.
If one dared to hope that under clause 36, with which we are now dealing, we might get a low rental housing project in Winnipeg it would soften the blow a bit so far as the other parts of the bill are concerned. But so long as this legislation makes it possible for the government of Manitoba to pass on part of its responsibility to the city, and so long as the percentage the federal government will pay is only 75 per cent, there is not much hope of getting a project of this nature in the city of Winnipeg. Nevertheless, despite its shortcomings, I agree with those who contend that publicity should be given to what is possible under clause 36, and that there should be as much educational work

National Housing Act
as possible so that the people of the country will get the best they can out of this inadequate legislation.
A moment ago I mentioned having read an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune. In addition I want to mention a news item which came to my attention last week. On Saturday evening at a quarter to seven I was across the hall in room 16 listening to and watching the television news. It so happens that included in the news at that time there was a brief shot of a Canadian soldier arriving from Korea by plane. I believe the picture was taken in Montreal where this soldier arrived after being flown back to this country. Why had he been flown back to Canada? Was it because of a tragedy on the field of battle? No, it was because he had lost a child who had been burned to death in his tar paper shack back here in Canada. I know the fuss that was raised in this house some weeks ago when one or two members of this group started talking about tar paper shacks. There are members on the other side who do not like references to that kind of housing. I suggest this house should take very seriously the fact that every year, every month, almost every week we see items in the news like the one to which I have just referred, where people lose their lives because of fires which take place because the houses in which they are living are fire traps that easily catch fire and burn down.
So far this clause, indeed this bill, does nothing to rectify that kind of situation. It does help to provide, sooner than otherwise would be the case, homes for certain people. But it does nothing for the group of people who really need homes, such as the soldier who had to leave his family in a tar paper shack with the result that one of his children was burned to death. Incidents such as that are a national scandal. There is no help in this clause or anywhere in this bill for such people. I submit that this parliament still has a long way to go in devising the kind of housing legislation that this country really needs.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 37-Powers of corporation.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
This clause,
Mr. Chairman, represents the last possible opportunity, I suppose, of amending this bill in such a way as to make it serve the purposes that are described on the front of the bill. Without some amendment to this clause, replacing the provision in the old act by which the government entered the field of housing on a joint loan basis, I submit

that the act at present represents the clear withdrawal of the government of Canada from the housing problem of this country.
It is true that the other day in a discussion of clause 11 I secured a tacit agreement from the minister that the government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, would be entering the field under that clause by the purchase of mortgages issued by the chartered banks. Now that may be so, Mr. Chairman, but unfortunately the legal authority for doing so limits the participation to the sum of $30 million. I believe the minister will agree with me that the two sections referred to, the one in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, and the other clause 22 of this bill, between them limit that participation to a total of $30 million.
I suggest that such participation is merely a drop in the bucket. I hope, before this bill is given third reading, the government will give serious consideration to the reenactment of that section of the old act under which the government really participated in the housing program in Canada. I want to point out that the figures presented to the banking and commerce committee showed that in the past the government's participation has been in the neighbourhood of $60 million under the joint loans program. There has been no definite statement from the government, and I am merely making an assumption since my suggestion was not denied on Friday, but I assume it is the government's intention to use clause 11 for this very minor feature of participation. I cannot put it more strongly than to say I feel the government has been disingenuous in the house here in the manner in which it has brought this legislation before parliament, which has resulted in a false impression in the public mind as to the purpose of this bill. Unless they are prepared to at least reinstate the provisions for participation, then I cannot see how this house can support such legislation, because it does not do what it purports to do on the front of the bill, that is, promote increased construction of houses in Canada.
The bill before us actually permits the government to withdraw from the very modest participation it had in the housing program of Canada, as set out in the old act. So I hope the government will see fit to maintain the very modest share it has taken in solving one of the important problems of this country.

Clause agreed to.

On clause 38-Contracts for houses to be sold to prospective home owners.

There are two avenues
through which the government can make loans for projects such as that envisaged by the hon. member for Churchill. National Housing Act
of the tender submitted by the contractor as the cost at which he will build a house. I am wondering whether that has some bearing on the matter.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: Has the corporation a policy, in places where they think building costs are higher than they might be, of setting lending values at a smaller percentage of the actual cost of construction than would be set in other centres?

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext: That is so, yes.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I can appreciate the corporation might wish to do what it can to keep building costs down. But surely the minister will agree with me that that inflicts a hardship upon those who live in those communities and wish to build houses there. Mr. Speaker, before this bill is given third reading I would like to state that I regret very much I cannot support it in many respects. While it purports to give some advantages to those seeking to build homes, I believe those advantages will not transpire. In fact, I think they will prove to be mere illusions.
It is said, for example, that there will be an advantage in the lower down payment. It is true a few dollars will be saved on the down payment but the interest rate will be 
higher, and any benefit which might accrue from a saving on the down payment will be swallowed up in the increased rate of interest over the years. All this bill presents is a hope on the part of the government that the banks will be induced to put some money into house building to replace the money which the government formerly supplied under the joint loan system, and possibly to make up for the money which the lending institutions may not advance in the future.
There is a hope, but there is very little evidence that there is much ground for that hope, and there is very little assurance that the banks will be sufficiently interested to put a sizeable amount of money into house building. Certainly there is no assurance that the 25 per cent which the government formerly put in under the joint loan system will be made up through loans advanced by the banks, and there is considerable evidence that the lending institutions may make fewer loans available than in the past.
The bill does not solve our housing problem. It will be just as difficult for those in the lower income groups to get houses after this bill becomes law as it was under the old act. It will also be equally difficult to get the provinces and the municipalities to cooperate with the federal government in the provisions under clause 36 as regards low rental housing. Evidence was given before the committee to the effect that there is considerable public apathy towards clause 36, and that the municipalities are loath to take advantage of it. Recommendations were made suggesting ways in which the government could improve clause 36 whereby the provinces and the municipalities could be induced to enter into an agreement with the federal government for the provision of low rental housing.
For those who need the houses most, this bill will be a disappointment. It will offer them very little more than the bill which it is designed to replace. One feature which I believe is open to criticism is that no one knows at this stage what the interest rates will be on loans. When the minister was asked whether he would consider fixing a limit for the interest rate and, if necessary, introducing a subsidy, we were told that that would be determined by government policy. But if there is any place in which government policy should be considered it is in this house now, before this bill is given third reading.
The government should continue subsidizing the interest rate, as it has been doing all through the years under the joint loan arrangement. It can do so, and it can fix a limit above which the interest rate will not go, and if necessary subsidize that interest rate just as it has been doing over the years.

Before this bill is given third reading, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill No. 102 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of amending it so as to provide a fixed limit as to the rate of interest to be charged on loans made under the provisions of the said act.
I know there will be criticism of this amendment on the ground that we are holding up an act which is necessary in order to enable us to get our spring building operations going; but this bill is going to determine the extent to which the people of Canada will be able to get houses not only this spring but next spring and possibly for years to come.
