He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for the revision and re-enactment of the Bank Act and for the renewal of existing bank charters for a further period of ten years. It is one of the most important items on the agenda of this session of parliament. At the same time I think it will be found that in its essential aspects it is a non-controversial bill. There will, of course, be differences of view on particular points, and various groups in the house will differ on the emphasis they place on certain parts of the bill. But if I gauge the sense of the house correctly there is general agreement that within the framework of our accepted economic structure our banking system is an excellent system; that it is efficient; it gives good service; it commands the confidence of the Canadian people; and it is highly regarded abroad.
I realize, of course, my hon. friends in the C.C.F. group believe that in due course, and as part of a general policy of socialization, the commercial banks should come under public ownership and operation. For those who accept their ultimate objective such a position is not illogical, but I take it

The Bank Act
that we are not at this time initiating a debate on socialism in general and that is why I suggest that in its essential aspects this is a non-controversial bill. It is nevertheless, as I have said, a very important bill.
I	hope, in fact, all interested members will consider it carefully and that it will receive careful and constructive scrutiny in the banking and commerce committee.
Before dealing with the bill itself, perhaps hon. members would be interested in a very brief statement on the history of banking in Canada. The first institution to offer full banking services in British North America was formed in 1817 in Montreal. The first Canadian bank to operate under a charter commenced business in Saint John, New Brunswick, in 1820.
At the time the first four provinces entered confederation, parliament endorsed and continued the charters of the provincially incorporated banks. At July 1, 1867, in the new Canada, there were 29 bank charters which were active or to become active. In addition there were three in Prince Edward Island and one in British Columbia.
Since confederation, 77 banks have obtained charters, of which 39 actually commenced business. The other 38 failed to open their doors to the public because, so far as can be ascertained, they were unable to raise sufficient capital.
In 1880 there were 36 banks in actual operation, 38 in 1890, 36 in 1900, 25 in 1913,
II	in 1923, 10 in 1934 and 1944, and at the present time there are 11.
Of the 72 banks which have operated under the Bank Act since confederation, 26 have failed and 35 have been absorbed by other banks. Of the 26 that failed, 13 were wound up without loss to noteholders or depositors. In the other 13 cases depositors suffered varying degrees of loss. While the losses suffered by the creditors and shareholders of some of the latter banks were unfortunate, they had a salutary effect. It compelled all other banks to strengthen their management and internal controls, and parliament from time to time passed legislation to improve the safeguards and protect the funds of depositors and shareholders. I should add that the last bank failure in Canada occurred more than 30 years ago. As hon. members know, our banking system weathered the economic storm of the 1930's in a manner of which we may well be proud.
The 11 banks which comprise our commercial banking system today have a combined age of almost 900 years, the oldest bank having been incorporated 136 years ago, and the youngest less than a year ago.

The latter incorporation was an important event in our banking history, as only one other bank-and that in 1929-has commenced business in Canada in over 40 years. With the exception of these two, each of our banks has been in business for over 80 years.
In 1871 the parliament of Canada passed its first bank act. One of its most important provisions was the extension of the charters for a period of ten years, and the consequential principle of a decennial revision of the Bank Act. It has been said that this period was chosen by agreement between the government and the bankers of the time, as both were of the opinion that there should be a periodic review of the legislation and of the manner in which the banking system was operating.
With the exception of four occasions, on which the charters were extended for one-year periods, because parliament wished to defer consideration of the act, there have been decennial extensions of charters ever since.
The principle of the decennial revision is an important one. It provides a good balance between stability and flexibility, between tradition and change. I am glad there is general agreement on this principle. Conditions in all countries change with the passage of time, and this is especially so in a rapidly expanding country like Canada.
In each decade as we review the Bank Act we ought to look both backward and forward; backward to see what weaknesses need to be remedied or what gaps need to be filled, and forward to make sure that our banking system has the capacity to meet the expanding needs and the changing circumstances of the future.
Ten years ago, in 1944, parliament gave careful study, not just to the Bank Act itself, but also to a group of related measures which, taken together, formed a coherent pattern for dealing with our expectations of the postwar period. In that year parliament not only revised the Bank Act, but it also created the industrial development bank, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Export Credits Insurance Corporation and passed the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Experience has shown that these were all good measures, and collectively they played a very large part in the relative smoothness of our post-war readjustments and in our progress and expansion since that time.
This year, in 1954, our legislative program in respect of banking is incorporated in four measures-the Bank of Canada Act amendments, the sections of the housing act relating to insured mortgages, the bill now before us,

and the act relating to the Quebec savings banks. The first two have already been approved in principle. I am now inviting the house to approve the third, and the last will be introduced shortly.
I thought we had a very useful discussion on the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill. I appreciated the thoughtful and moderate speech of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). He will not expect me to agree with all the implications of his remarks or with the precise balance of his emphasis. But I felt it was a good speech, that it recorded a useful degree of progress toward a mutual understanding of these matters, and I am glad to accept his invitation to deal briefly with the fundamental points he raised. He mentioned nine major factors which determine the course of economic progress and prosperity, and he concluded that they could be pretty well summed up in the dominant role of the regulation of the volume of bank deposits. The control of bank credit is, of course, a very important matter; but I would not be prepared to go as far as my friend from Peace River when he says, or implies, that if you look after bank deposits everything else will take care of itself.
It seems to me that steady and sustained economic progress depends upon two broad sets of factors. One is monetary, the other is non-monetary. The non-monetary factors include such basic things as the skill and efficiency of our people in applying their energies to our available resources. Constantly improving productivity is essential. Without it the most ingenious and efficient monetary arrangements will not get us very far. Skill, energy and efficiency together with confidence, integrity and a spirit of adventure-these are the foundations of economic progress.
But in a complex economic society sound monetary arrangements are also essential. I agree that the control and regulation of bank credit is important, but I would not assign it such an overriding importance as does the hon. member for Peace River. I prefer to think in terms of three related and interlocking factors: 1, the variation in cash reserves with its effects on bank credit and bank deposits; 2, the interest rate structure, with its effects on saving and spending and on the allocation of productive resources among the many competing claims; and 3, the effects of over-all fiscal policy. None of these are independent variables, each reacts upon the others; and the essential task of monetary and fiscal policy is to harmonize these several factors and use them to direct and encourage the economy as a whole in the right direction and at the most desirable pace. There are
The Bank Act
times and circumstances when major reliance should be placed upon fiscal policy; at other times the brakes should be applied or relaxed chiefly through variations in cash reserves; at still other times or places influencing the interest rate structure, as a whole or at some point, may be the most sensible approach. I do not think you can generalize for all times or for all circumstances.
In other words the administration of monetary policy requires a high degree of skill and good judgment. It requires selecting the right means or combination of means, and applying those means at the right time and place and in just about the right degree. For this, there is no simple formula.
One last point, before I leave these general considerations. There is a tendency in general monetary discussions to overlook the international elements in the problem. Too often the argument is developed in relation to what economists, I believe, call "a closed economy". Canada, of course, is almost the very opposite to a closed economy. We live by trade and are exposed to all the economic winds of the world around us. We cannot hope, indeed we should not wish, to insulate ourselves against the world.
This means two things. First, we can never expect to be free from a certain amount of economic ups and downs transmitted to us from abroad; and, second, for that very reason we should assist wherever possible in promoting sensible international trade and monetary co-operation, while at the same time keeping our own economy as efficient and as flexible as possible in both its physical and monetary aspects.
I turn now to the substance of the bill before us. I shall not attempt, nor would it be in accordance with the rules, to deal with all the numerous changes proposed. A great many of these are technical, some of them indeed purely verbal to improve the language or clarify the meaning. I shall deal first with changes of substance or principle which will affect the general public.
One of the most important amendments proposed is a change in the method of calculating the cash reserves of a bank and the minimum rate thereof. I referred to this change at some length when speaking on the amendments to the Bank of Canada Act, and I am sure it is not necessary to repeat all of the explanations which I gave at that time. The minimum cash reserve ratio is to be increased to 8 per cent of Canadian dollar deposit liabilities and, as hon. members will recall, there is an amendment proposed in the Bank of Canada Act to permit the Bank of Canada to vary that rate from time to time, within a range of 8 to 12 per cent. The basis

The Bank Act
of calculation is to be changed to a monthly average instead of the daily basis now in effect. This will permit much more flexibility, as a bank may allow its cash reserve ratio to fall below the minimum rate for several days to meet temporary emergencies, providing that it reaches the required average over the entire month.
Another important amendment relates to the power of banks to lend on insured mortgages. The first bank act of 1871 prohibited the banks from lending money on the security of mortgages on real or immovable property, and this prohibition has remained in subsequent acts. There is no doubt that during the early development stages of this country, with a high loss factor and the lack of liquidity of mortgage investments at certain periods, this was a wise provision and contributed greatly to the safety record of the banks. The Farm Improvement Loans Act in 1944 and the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act in 1946 provided that, notwithstanding anything in the Bank Act, a bank was authorized, under certain circumstances, to make a guaranteed loan on the security of a mortgage. This house has just completed consideration of a revision of the National Housing Act, of which one of the principal features is authority to the banks to lend money for residential construction on the security of mortgages insured by a government agency.
This major change in bank legislation was given very careful consideration before it was proposed to parliament and it is believed that with the insurance, amortization requirements and other liquidity features, this type of mortgage lending will become a safe investment for a portion of the bank funds and will provide a useful additional source of funds for this very important sector of the economy of our country.
It has been suggested in some quarters that a limit should be placed upon the aggregate amount that a bank may lend on this type of security, but I am not in favour of a restriction of this kind. A limit established by legislation is likely to become a target, either for the lender or for those who wish more to be loaned. Conditions will alter from time to time as between one bank and another and for the system as a whole, and I prefer to leave this matter to the good judgment of those whose duty it is to invest wisely the funds entrusted to them.
For some years the banks, by means of loans, have been assisting materially in the development of the country's oil resources. When the act was drafted in 1944 this part of a bank's business was relatively unimportant, and the provisions relating to the

security which may be taken for such loans are not entirely satisfactory under present-day conditions. To permit the banks to give to this very important industry the measure of financial support which is required, a new section containing very extensive provisions has been inserted in the bill.
Section 88 of the Bank Act is a unique piece of banking legislation. Some of its provisions have a history in Canadian banking which commenced long before confederation. In changing form it has carried the same section number in each act since 1913. I believe that, for the most part, it has proven satisfactory in its present form and the only change I am proposing at this time in the lending provisions is authority to the banks to lend money to farmers for the purchase of seed potatoes. In the other provisions regarding notices of intention to give security, several changes have been made on the recommendations of the banks and Bank of Canada. These relate almost entirely to the routine of filing, registration, release and cancellation of such notices, and are intended to enable the Bank of Canada to dispose of obsolete records and notices.
The Bank Act of 1871 authorized the banks, with certain restrictions, to issue notes for circulation in Canada, and in 1897 authority was given for the issue of notes in any British possession outside Canada where the bank had a branch and where this was not contrary to the laws of the country. After the advent of the Bank of Canada in 1935 the chartered banks' note issues were gradually withdrawn. In January, 1950, the banks paid to the Bank of Canada approximately $13J million, an amount equal to their outstanding Canadian notes, and thereafter the Bank of Canada became liable to redeem the notes on presentation. With this payment the additional liability, often referred to as the "double liability", which formerly attached to a bank's shares in proportion to its outstanding note issue, was extinguished.
For many years the cost of foreign note issue including taxes has made this an unprofitable operation, and the banks have been reducing the outstanding amount as occasion has permitted. It is now approximately equivalent to $130,000. The bill before you provides that all note-issuing privileges of the banks shall cease and also for methods of retiring the foreign note circulation now outstanding.
I turn next to a group of amendments relating to the incorporation and the share capital of banks. I am proposing an amendment to provide that if parliament is not

sitting during the last month of the ten-year period for which this act authorizes the banks to carry on business the authority is extended until 60 days after the next session commences. This, of course, is meant solely as a safeguard in case parliament should rise before or during that last month without dealing with this act and thus leave the banks without authority to carry on.
Another amendment is to increase the amount of capital that a newly-incorporated bank must have before it commences business. The present requirements are a minimum subscribed capital of $500,000 and a minimum paid-up capital of $250,000. These requirements were established in 1890, and with the greatly increased costs likely to be incurred in bringing a bank into profitable operation under today's conditions a larger amount of initial capital is considered necessary. In this bill the minimum subscribed capital is stated at $1,000,000 and the minimum paid-up capital at $500,000.
With the rapid and very substantial growth in the assets of the banks during the past few years it has become desirable for some of them to obtain new capital. There are difficulties attached to making a new issue of capital stock under the provisions of the present act if the bank has shareholders resident in countries where considerable detailed information must be filed before the issue of capital stock by a foreign bank is approved. An amendment to the present procedure with respect to the allotment of new stock which will help to overcome this obstacle is proposed.
When there was additional liability attached to the bank shares for the purpose of protecting the note issue it was essential that the shares could be transferred only by registration on the books of the bank. This protection is no longer necessary, and a proposed amendment authorizes each bank, if it so wishes, to provide by bylaw for another method of share transfer.
The present act provides for the procedure when one bank purchases all or part of the assets of another bank. Because of legislation which imposes a tax on the undistributed income of a corporation when it is wound up, a bank which is solvent but recognizes that its future may be limited is, in effect, prevented from joining with another bank. Section 100 of this bill provides a procedure for the amalgamation of two banks and their continuance thereafter as a single entity. _
Hon. members will find in this bill several changes in the provisions relating to the financial statements and periodic returns made by the banks. These changes, intended
The Bank Act
to clarify and improve the information in the statements and returns, have been made after consideration of recommendations received from the banks and their auditors.
At present the banks are required to file an annual return of unclaimed deposits, drafts and accepted cheques after they have remained unpaid for a period of five years and each year thereafter until they are paid to the owner or to the Bank of Canada in trust. The returns now filed contain as many as
25.000	names. They require a substantial amount of work to prepare and, as far as can be ascertained, relatively few payments to creditors have resulted therefrom.
I am proposing in this bill that the returns contain only the details of amounts unclaimed for a period of over nine years, that is, one year before they are paid to the Bank of Canada in trust, if still unclaimed. The returns will then contain between 4,500 and
5.000	names, and it is provided that this information will be published in the Canada Gazette. It is hoped that publication will result in more amounts being returned to their rightful owners.
At the time of the 1944 revision of this act it was provided that the banks should make an annual return of earnings and expenses in a form which now appears in the act as schedule Q. A compilation for all banks of these returns and of the averages for 15 years has since been tabled annually in parliament and published in the Canada Gazette. Hon. members will, no doubt, have noticed the last statement in the Canada Gazette of February 13 of this year.
When the 15-year period was chosen for the return it was not considered sufficiently long to present a fair basis for average figures of earnings, expenses and losses, but as there was no relative information available with respect to the banks which ceased to operate during the twenties, this was the longest period for which reliable comparative figures could be obtained.
I am now proposing a change in schedule Q to lengthen the period of averages to 25 years, which is considered a more suitable basis for a report of this kind.
In that connection, I believe hon. members would be interested in a few comparative figures which indicate the growth of our banking system in the last quarter century. At the end of 1928 the banks reported total assets of approximately $3,470 million. At December 31, 1953, the reported assets had expanded almost threefold and amounted to $10,140 million.
The following figures give the distribution of profits for the average of the 25 financial years of the banks ending in 1953: Profits

The Bank Act
after taxes, but before losses and provision for losses on investments, loans, and other assets amounted to $36-6 million. That is dealt with in the following manner:
Dividends paid to shareholders, $14 million. Additions to profit and loss accounts and to rest accounts including amounts retransferred from contingency reserves, net, $3-5 million.
Losses and provision for losses on investments, loans and other assets, net, $12-4 million.
Additions to contingency reserves, net, $6-7 million.
It will be noted that the latter figure of $6-7 million is about 21- per cent of the $266-8 million average increase in assets for the same period.
As the house is aware, it is my responsibility under the Income Tax Act to inform the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) if, in my opinion, transfers in any year to the contingency reserves of a bank are excessive. There have been very few occasions in the past ten years when this has occurred. The total of such excess transfers for all banks in the fiscal years 1944 and 1945 amounted to $378,000, on which full taxes were paid. Subject to final audit of the reports for the fiscal years ending in 1953, no excess transfers have been made by the banks in any of the last eight years.
Finally, there are certain changes relating to the internal management of the banks' affairs which should be mentioned. The present act requires the pension funds of the banks to be invested in securities in which a trustee may invest under the Trust Companies Act. A bank pension fund is usually under the management of. a board consisting of the directors and members of the staff of the bank, and is maintained in part by contributions from the staff and to a greater extent by contributions from the bank. It is the practice to have an actuarial survey of the fund at least once in every five years, and for the bank to make up any deficiencies which occur because of changing rates of income and other factors. In my opinion the management of these funds should be left to those concerned, and I am recommending that the present investment restrictions be withdrawn with the exception that no contribution be permitted to a fund that invests in bank stocks.
There are changes also in the provisions relating to the bank auditors. It is now usual for bank auditors to act in an advisory capacity with respect to many matters outside the scope of a normal audit, such as income tax returns, capital stock issues and accounting methods and routines, and it is provided that they may be engaged for and remunerated for such special work, if it is approved by the directors of the bank.

In the 1944 act provision was made for destruction of bank records in which the entries had been made more than 30 years before. The accumulation and storage of a vast quantity of paid cheques and obsolete records has become a major problem with the banks, and it is now proposed to reduce to 20 years the period for which such documents are to be kept, with a provision that the signature cards and other identification records pertaining to an account transferred to the Bank of Canada in trust shall be kept as long as they are required.
There are a great number of changes from the 1944 act in this bill consequential upon some of those to which I have referred. In particular, the elimination of the provisions relating to note issues has meant a redrafting and redistribution of a great many of the sections in the act. None of these make any important changes of substance or of principle, and therefore require no explanation at this time. At the conclusion of this debate I propose to move that this bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee, where hon. members will be able to obtain all the detailed information and explanations they may require.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I can sum up by saying that the only really important changes of principle in this decennial revision of the Bank Act relate to cash reserves and lending on insured mortgages. These changes themselves are not new or untried developments. They flow naturally from our own experience and from the experience of other reasonably comparable countries. They follow the precepts of "conservative innovation" and the "matching of new institutions to old" described nearly a century ago by that great authority on English banking, Walter Bagehot.
That the experience of the last ten years, which has included such confused, difficult and complex problems as well as such an unprecedented rate of Canadian growth and development, should require so few major changes is a tribute both to the wisdom of our predecessors in parliament and to the skill and integrity of those responsible for the operation of our banking system. Canada has been well served both by its central bank and by its chartered banks. Doubtless there have been faults in the past, and faults of degree or of timing can hardly be avoided in the future, for banking and monetary management will always be matters of skill and judgment and a careful assessment of risks.
Whether we look back 10, 50 or 80 years, I think we can be proud of the Canadian banking system which has developed with

the country, adapted itself to our own conditions, learned from its past mistakes, and steadily expanded in size, strength and flexibility, and in the confidence it commands both at home and abroad.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all listened with great interest to the minister's review of the situation. We can agree fully with him as to the importance of this measure, and we can agree also with the wisdom of having this decennial review.
I understand it was established some short time after confederation when it was felt both by the government and the banks that it was well worth while to have this periodic review in order to assess what had been done, to take stock of the situation, and to see what changes required to be made.
The review of ten years ago contained a good deal of spirited argumentation not merely because there were some views from the gentlemen on my far left, but also because on the government side itself very strong views developed among some of its members as to the inexpediency of some of the provisions of the act.
I shall not deal at any length with what the minister said today. The points he raised will naturally come before the committee. I agree fully with what he said at the conclusion of his remarks, namely that the two important things in the bill are the cash reserves and the new powers to make mortgage loans. Without pursuing the matter further, may I say that I was struck with what seemed to me to be a superficial inconsistency. I stress the word "superficial", because it may be that in committee I shall be constrained to change my mind. I notice that the minister on the one hand said that he was not in favour of fixing any limit in connection with mortgage loans to be made by the banks. That emphasized what had been in my mind already, namely just why in the matter of the cash reserves it is felt necessary to become more rigid and mechanical. I raise the question as to the ratio of reserves which, through the practice of decades-one might almost say of centuries -has proved a satisfactory working arrangement. Why does this now need to be altered in the way proposed? But that is a matter for the committee.
Any temptation I might have had to indulge in a historical review I think has been entirely swept away, because the minister himself has given us a good many interesting points in connection with early banking. There is only one point I wish to make. Though in fact I think our banking system
The Bank Act
may be said, in the main, to follow the Scottish system, nevertheless I read to my interest in the Macmillan report:
It is generally agreed that the Canadian banking system is a direct descendant of the first bank of the United States . . .
I read that with interest. The report goes on to say that in the charter of the Bank of Montreal, which was the first charter, actually a considerable amount of wording from this United States bank charter was to be found. I mention that fact purely as a matter of interest.
The minister has also dealt with the disappearance of the double liability which used to be such a great feature of our banking system, and has explained that it has disappeared as the individual bank notes have disappeared. I recall one interesting historical point. When the banks were free to issue notes there was a special provision by which they could increase the note issue for the moving of the wheat crop, for which privilege, incidentally, they paid a special tax.
As we pause for a moment to reflect on our banking service, it seems to me to be worth while to remind ourselves what an amazing service it really is, if you take time to consider that we can send money almost anywhere in the world practically instantaneously, even by telegraph if we wish to do so, and that it costs us nothing but a four-cent stamp-no, I mean a five-cent stamp-to send a cheque, when we pay by cheque. It seems to me that the service is one that we have become so accustomed to that we forget actually what an amazing convenience it is that almost within a stone's throw of each of us we have a fully equipped banking service which can do business for us anywhere in the world.
In the second place I think we are fortunate to have 11 competing banks. The minister has already referred to the new bank that came in this year, namely the Mercantile Bank, with a Dutch background. I think we are fortunate to have this addition to our financial equipment, because actually they bring in a background of experience somewhat different from that of our own banks. Of course behind regulating, advising and sometimes virtually controlling the actions of the chartered banks, we have the Bank of Canada which has now been in existence for 20 years and which has rendered services that we all know about.
I want to say a word about one aspect of our banking system which I think is of vast importance, namely our branch system. We realize that it was a tremendous strength

The Bank Act
to us in the early thirties when United States banks were going down like ninepins. In our system of a small number of banks with a large number of branches we are really like an army with many divisions, with a general reserve available for all. Although legal arrangements have strengthened their position in the last few years, the United States banks at one time really had to carry their own reserves, with the results that we saw only too unhappily in 1932. Of course it was a well-known fact that many United States banks which then had to close their doors had plenty of assets but were not able to realize them quickly enough.
I now want to add a sentence or two about early banking in order to recall to our minds that in the beginning, banking really was just custody of property. Men of reputation and probity were asked to take care of the valuables of other people. That was the way it began. To deposit merely meant leaving valuables with a dependable person. Next came discount; that was the purpose of bills of exchange. Then last of all there was the question of issue, and along with it came the development of payment by cheque. All of this was completed by the end of the seventeenth century and that virtually set us up with banking as we know it today.
As I say, the business of banking began with deposits. The lifeblood of banks is deposits. We cannot walk a hundred yards in any of our cities without seeing advertisements urging us to deposit our money in banks. As we know, that raises questions which I do not propose to delve into here. I am not going to pronounce judgment as to whether we lend deposits or the proceeds of deposits. Those who have the time to read the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee of ten years ago will find that that was a question which was argued at that time. The one thing I wish to stress is that the conception we seem sometimes to run across, namely that the banks have piled up in a corner huge amounts of money that they might lend if they wished, is something we must get away from. We must try to clear our minds, at any rate, and to remember that deposits are liabilities of the bank.
If you take any bank statement, here is what you will find. I have here the statement of one of the larger banks. If you look at the asset side you will find first of all that there is some $600 million cash or its equivalent; then there are $1,700 million of government and other securities. Following that there are some $700 million of current loans. On the other side, the liability side, you will find a liability which overshadows all other

liabilities-indeed it is about nine-tenths of the whole of the liabilities-namely the deposits, amounting in this case to $2,527 million. I am just raising this point, Mr. Speaker, because it seems to me that we should try to have a clear view as to what is the situation when we talk about loans.
I want to say just one word about credit. Much excitement has been caused from time to time by misunderstanding of the banks' function of creating credit. Banks do create credit. I want to read a brief word on credit from the budget speech of Mr. Dunning in April of 1939. As reported at page 3144 of Hansard of that year he said:
The policy which has been followed has been one designed to expand money and credit as rapidly as the needs of the public require, but not so rapidly as to create an unhealthy, speculative expansion which would be bound to end in a serious depression.
What really happens is that when banks create credit, what they do is, as it were, to turn into money, in advance, goods which are going to be created. Let us consider the situation, for example, in the fall of 1939. We all remember what the position was then. There had been a good deal of unemployment. Then we ran into a situation where goods were needed, materials were available, labour was available and purchasers were available. Then what do we find? We find that in the autumn of 1939 Mr. Ilsley brought in a budget in which he indicated that there was going to be $156 million-I think that is the figure- of a deficit deliberately incurred because it was necessary to stimulate business and get things started.
Let me give a simple case. You have a man who owns a stone quarry. Nearby is a line of railway which needs rock ballast. The owner of the quarry goes to the bank and states his case. He has the material and he has the labour. Transportation is available, a market is available, and he wants to borrow $100,000. The bank examine the situation. They have expert, skilled people who are able to estimate potential value. Let us assume that the bank considers the potential new wealth sufficient for repayment and a loan is granted. What is the result? The result is that the bank's assets and liabilities are both increased by the amount of the loan. On the asset side is the borrower's note; on the liability side is the new deposit. If the stone quarry succeeds the note will be repaid, which means that the wealth which has been created has, so to speak, caught up with the credit which was created in order to enable it to be done. Always, of course, the bank

must have regard to its cash position, to its cash reserves held by itself and with the central bank.
There is another point I should like to make. The only way the banks have to earn money is to make loans. They are in business to lend as much as possible. That is the only source of their income. Sometimes people talk as if, somehow or other, the banks did not want to make loans, as if they were holding back and sitting on large sums of money which they did not want to lend. Of course that is absurd. The average bank manager wants to have his loans just as large as he safely can. The view is apparently held that in some way or other the banks can, by some magic process which I have never been able to understand, go ahead and really take the place of government. I want to read an extract from a speech made the other day by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and also one from a speech made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), both of whom we often hear in the house. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said, as recorded at page 2660 of Hansard for March 4:
. . . public ownership and control of the commercial banks is necessary if we are going to have complete control by the people over fiscal and monetary policies. We recognize and contend that those who control fiscal and monetary policies exercise tremendous control over the lives of our people.
The hon. member for Assiniboia said, as found at page 2661 of Hansard for March 4: . . . there is no assurance that when the nation is facing the possibility of a recession the chartered banks will do that which is in the interest of the nation at that time, namely, make the borrowing of money easier.
I want to make one or two comments on these statements because it seems to me they are all wrong, and that there is no justification for the views put forward. There is no justification for the view that the banks are going to hold back. But if I were the head of a bank I would not want to have to explain to the hon. member for Assiniboia, who is a big, strong fellow, that I had made so many bad loans I could not repay his deposit. In other words, when a banker is making a loan he has to have regard to his liabilities, particularly his cash, when he has a liability to a big, able-bodied man. I ask most seriously whether the hon. members to whom I have referred have thought this matter over in a really serious manner. I have tried to think it over, and I present my views for what they are worth.
I have tried to ask myself what would happen if the banks were nationalized. Let
The Bank Act
us imagine the banks nationalized. What happens the next day? You have the same men presumably, the same assets presumably, and very little change in personnel. The bank managers will be reporting to the same seniors to begin with, at any rate, but I submit that a change has taken place. I submit that we now have men who have become civil servants, who are subject to rigid legal requirements and strict regulations and are liable to criticism if they depart from them in any way. As far as these men are concerned, I suggest that actually it will probably not be easier but harder to get loans. I suggest there will be a new rigidity coming into the situation.
The other day I was struck by something said to me by a senior and very able official of one of the crown companies. He has come to his post from private business, and he said to me, "People come to me and want to make deals with me". He said, "They suggest to me that after all I need not be very tightly bound by legislation and that I could use my discretion". He said, "I cannot; I am bound by legislation". I think he was right.
In my own mind I was trying to compare his very senior position with that of the general manager of a chartered bank. He will have regulations to guide him, and of course he has a board of directors to whom he is responsible; but I suggest that he is a very much freer agent than my friend, the senior official of a crown company. I suggest that within a reasonable range he will be expected to use his discretion. Indeed, if he were tied and afraid ever to step a little to the right or to the left of strict regulation I suggest that his board of directors would tell him that he was not the man for their money at all. They would expect him to take responsibility and, as I say, to use his discretion.
That is the situation on the one side. Incidentally, so far as nationalizing the banks is concerned, I am going to point out in a moment that the socialists in England are apparently entirely cured of the desire, which I think they did have 20 years ago, to socialize the joint stock banks.
I want to come back to a second and what I think is a worse danger on the other side. I refer to the danger of political interference. Let us be candid and honest with each other. Let us assume there is a large company operating in a small town where it provides most of the employment. Let us suppose it has got into real difficulty and let us imagine the situation with the chartered banks as they are now and if you had them under government auspices.

The Bank Act
If you have proper management of the chartered banks, as we have now, what will you find? You will find that there is every desire to help that company if it can properly be done, but nevertheless you will find that in the last analysis the matter will be decided on sound business principles because the officials of the bank always have in the back of their minds the strong obligation they owe to the depositors whose money they have. Now let us assume that you have the banks nationalized and let us assume, as I say, that you have this business operating in a small community where it is vital to the lifeblood of the community. Am I being unfair, am I being cynical if I say it is just not possible that the local member of parliament will not be approached and pressured to see that that company gets its loan? As a result the transaction will not be carried out on the basis of strict business principles.
Therefore it is my feeling that you would have two undesirable factors. First of all you would have an area in which there is rigidity, and in which loans will perhaps not be made as freely as they are now. Second, you would have an area which politics would certainly try to invade. I need not say that if loans are made on political principles I would be prepared to predict disaster in the end.
Here I mention again the English socialists. The Bank of England was nationalized. I have no criticism to make of that. I think the control of credit should be, as is the case in Canada now, in national hands. But the Bank of England, just as the Bank of Canada, does not engage in the conduct of ordinary business. It leaves that to the joint stock banks of England. They are not interfered with in their ordinary operations by the Bank of England. The English socialists have accepted that. I was talking to a well-informed economist from England the other day, and he said he thought the English socialists believe it is a good thing to have competition among the joint stock banks.
I submit further that in those two extracts I read from the speeches of the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre what they really wanted, whether or not they intended it, was the chartered banks to step outside their own prerogatives and undertake what is the business of the government. If business has to be stimulated, if projects have to be carried on which will stimulate activity, that is a matter for the government and not for the chartered banks. The banks are there to safeguard the interests of their depositors and, within that proviso of course, to make loans just as freely as they possibly can.

I want to say a word or two about the conditions facing our banks today, because it seems to me that they may be in difficulty. We have had 15 years of boom. Prices have been going up. Nearly everybody has made money, although failures are beginning to show up now. The banks have had really a rather easy time, you might say. It is always easy when prices are going up, provided they are not soaring in a wild, crazy fashion. As I say, the banks have had a rather easy time. Whether or not it is going to continue to be so easy we are not so sure at the moment. There is hesitation today. There is fear of what might happen in the United States. In the United States it is being said that March is their deadline. The other day our own Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) said this was an anxious time.
I want to take just a moment or two to indicate what I think are the processes of mind through which a banker goes when he is making a loan. He has, of course, to study the business. He must have a complete knowledge of the conditions affecting the borrower. I want to read just a word or two from an article appearing in the Globe and Mail of last Saturday by Wellington Jeffers pointing out, in what I thought was an interesting way, the extent to which the banks had organized themselves in connection with the new loans to which the minister referred this afternoon and to which section 82 will relate. He said:
Some of the main banks have developed complete organizations for geological and statistical study of every new field and of the operations of companies working in it. They have their own geologists and a banker on this sort of work soon becomes one of the chief experts. All this organization is to enable the banks in this booming but speculative business to decide where loans would be justified because of hopeful operations and for the protection of the money loaned.
Then he goes on to say:
The geologist of one of the great New York banks told me that this is one of the active lending sectors of United States banks and is based on geological studies which can now make clear in a proved, developing field how much oil or gas is below the ground just as much in many cases as though they were stored above ground.
This interested me, because it seemed to show at once the thoroughness and initiative which banks do show in helping the development of business in a country.
The banker must know, of course, in the case of a manufacturing business what is the productive capacity of the total industry in Canada, so as to be able to judge what competition his borrower is going to have. He must know something about the home

market, the export market and competitive conditions both at home and abroad. He will be concerned, for example, with a remark made by Mr. Muir of the Royal Bank the other day. He said:
Startling and unpleasant as it may be. however, there is evidence also that Canada is tending to become a high cost economy in which natural and artificial barriers prevent us from achieving the degree of flexibility and mobility required for orderly adjustment. One marked evidence of this inflexibility is to be found in the failure of retail prices to reflect the general fall, since 1951, in the prices of raw materials.
He will be concerned with another remark made by Mr. Muir to this effect:
It was with this possibility in mind that I felt obliged last year to voice some doubts about the permanence of a prosperity built so largely on the "treacherous sands of consumer credit".
I am just trying, Mr. Speaker, to indicate how, as I see it, the banker views his business and the extent to which he must be an expert in conditions today. When I say "banker" of course I am thinking not only of the branch manager but of the senior officials right to the top, where he gets the most expert assistance available.
He will also have particularly to consider conditions in the United States. Are our prices really higher than those in the United States? Is it true that United States tourists no longer buy our goods when they come here because the prices are so high? Then he would, of course, consider the question of the premium on our money; that is a problem. It is a problem which, of course, is costing our manufacturers and exporters a great deal. For example, the newsprint people get paid in United States dollars and then have to take a sizeable discount. The same condition applies to other industries as well. This condition curtails exports and stimulates imports. It flatters our ego, perhaps, but it picks our pockets a bit, too. It is brought about by the fact that the interest rate is lower in the United States, and that stimulates borrowing in New York. Competent people fear that this premium may stimulate borrowing causing it to go higher, and that would act as a brake on business.
I repeat that the stimulus about which we are talking, and about which the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) talked particularly, must come from the government and not from the banks. The banks have their proper duty to perform, but it is not that of a government. I want to say, too, a word about money management, though of course that is primarily the concern of the Bank of Canada. I do not believe it can be stressed too often that the only safeguard we have is the wisdom and foresight of the people in
The Bank Act
charge of the Bank of Canada and their power, if necessary, to withstand political pressure.
This raises the question I raised at the time we dealt with the Bank of Canada Act. It is a difficult and perplexing question, I admit, but could we have some kind of automatic check put in the Bank of Canada Act? There was such a check in the original act, but it has been nullified by subsequent legislation. Were we wrong when we put it in the Bank of Canada Act? Is it true that any check becomes meaningless when we go into the business of managing money?
I believe that it is a very important question for the committee to consider. Should there be some kind of check? Should there be some way by which the Bank of Canada, if it wished to take a stand against government policy, could do so? Let us assume that a time arises when the government is under great pressure, as the United States government has been. They started in with what they called a hard money policy, but they have taken flight from it so far as I can make out. They have had to put the shoe on the other foot. The Macmillan commission, composed of thoroughly able men, recommended a check. The question is whether the committee should come back with a recommendation that some check should be provided.
It is fair, I think, to remind ourselves that money management is a tricky business. We had a good deal of experience with it in 1946 and 1947, and later when we were managing our money to the extent of fixing the value of it rather than leaving it free. We remember that in 1946 the dollar was put back to par at a time when subsequent events showed it was not worth par. We remember that in 1947 we lost $1,150 million in reserves. We remember that in the autumn of that year drastic action was taken, what some of us called legislation by radio. We remember that a prohibition against certain imports was imposed, and I think it is fair to say also that these drastic restrictions gave an amount of protection far beyond any tariff. It was absolute protection, and it stimulated the development of certain industries in a rather extravagant fashion. It may be that, in the long run, it was not a very desirable thing. These restrictions were finally removed, but by that time we had these industries which had been built up under this absolute ban on imports.
There is one other thing to which I want to refer because it has always amazed me, having regard to the main concern, and that is that we went through a period here when there was a belief we could control interest

The Bank Act
rates. When I look back to the men concerned, for whom I have great respect, it is almost impossible for me to realize how they got themselves into that state of mind, but they did. I want to read briefly into the record a statement made in October, 1945, in connection with the sale of victory bonds:
Of course, when you buy victory bonds you don't know for sure just when you may need to turn them into cash. Perhaps you will wait until they mature.
I should say this statement from which I am reading was an official statement and has in it statements made by the then minister of finance and one of the senior officials of the finance department.
Perhaps you will wait until they mature. Perhaps you can't wait that long. What happens then?
Most Canadians know the answer to this question. They know victory bonds can be turned into cash at any time. To meet temporary needs for cash, they can be used, as security for a bank loan. To meet other needs, they can be sold through any bank, investment dealer, stock broker, or trust company. The current market value of the bonds, with interest up to the day of sale, is paid to you while you wait. It's as simple as that.
And then I shall read the statement from the bank, which says this:
Government bond prices reflect the level of interest rates. A decline in bond prices could happen only if interest rates were to rise. In my opinion, the needs of the future will require and enable the kind of monetary policy which has brought about the current level of interest rates. Continuance of this policy means stability in victory bond prices.
Having read that, hon. members will not be surprised to learn that many people went about saying the treasury had positively made the statement that 3 per cent bonds would not go below par. It was the easiest thing in the world for a salesman, in view of what I have just read, to go one-tenth of one per cent farther.
I think it was in January of 1947 when bonds were allowed to go down two or three points in price. They had been at 105, and they came down to around 102. I was travelling with a man who was quite well up in the bond business in Toronto. Referring to this drop in the price of bonds I said to him, "Is nature going to be allowed to take its course?" He said, "Perhaps; but of course, bonds cannot go below par." I said, "Why not?' He said, "Because Mr. Ilsley said they could not." I said, "I do not think you will find that Mr. Ilsley did say that." Here was a man with some competency in his profession who held that view.
I have said just a word about the minister's remarks on increased reserves. I think I should add no more on that. The matter will come before the committee in due course.
(Mr. Macdonnell.]
Another point we will have to discuss in committee is that of convertibility, and I think I need not add anything further on that point.
As to the new provisions concerning mortgage loans, I think that has been fully discussed and I shall say nothing further about it, except that it is so long since liquidity was considered a matter of any importance that I feel that, while we expect the banks to co-operate fully-and I am sure they will, so far as they can-on the other hand, simply because we have gone through so many years with liquidity, practically so remote that it was like a subject that is discussed only in textbooks, we should not allow ourselves to forget that the primary obligation of a bank is to be able to pay back its depositors. We must keep in mind that these restrictions were put on by men who were considered wise and prudent in their dealings, and that they have prevailed for many years.
The governor of the Bank of Canada said frankly the other day that for some time he had held the opinion that banks might be allowed to make mortgage loans. Nevertheless I hope we will never reach the point where pressure is put on the banks to go beyond that point which they themselves consider prudent.
Having said this I think, Mr. Speaker, that I shall permit the matter to go to the committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has already been said, the decennial revision of the bank charters act and, of course, the motion now before us, together provide an opportunity for the house to make some review of the policies followed by the chartered banks and to suggest such improvements and changes as from the experience of members of the house and the country generally would seem to be desirable. That is the purpose of the decennial review of charters.
I am going to say at once that the Canadian banks have a very impressive record of efficient management, of safety and of profit to their shareholders. I shall offer some criticism of their operations in relation to the public and national interest, but I shall keep what I have just said in mind, because I think one should do so. In discussing this measure I shall not refer specifically to the criticism made of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue)

by the hon. member lor Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I think he will see in what I am about to say an inherent defence of what they said the other day.
Traditionally the concept of the responsibility of the commercial banker in this, as in other countries, has been a relatively simple one. That is, his responsibility can be considered to have been, in his view, a comparatively simple one. In the past it was generally recognized and widely accepted that the banker's responsibility was, first, to safeguard the interests of the depositors and of the institution itself. And this, I say at once, Canadian banks as a whole have done well. His second function, he considered, was to use the proceeds of the deposits to make loans and investments calculated to give the best results to the shareholders of the banks.
Hon. members will note that I said "to use the proceeds of the deposits", not necessarily the deposits. For I have in mind the undisputed fact-which I am sure the hon. member who has just taken his seat and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will not dispute- that loans from banks, or a bank's ability to loan, to put it in perhaps a better way, are both only in part based upon deposits, and as well of course on the reserves of the bank, rather than on the actual amount of the deposits. That is, loans are not limited to the actual amounts on deposit in the keeping of the various banks. In other words, banks do create credit. I think that is generally agreed.
In modern times, then, banks have not loaned moneys actually deposited by the public; rather they have based the extent of their loans in relation to their deposits and reserves. In other words they have created credit and created new money several times in excess of the actual funds in their possession, if you consider credit to be a form of money, knowing that at no one time would all the depositors demand the repayment of all their deposits but only a fraction of them.
This bill, like the Bank of Canada Act we discussed a short time ago, restricts these privileges to a greater extent than heretofore under our legislation. As has already been said, the safety of the Canadian banking system has been largely due to the fact that it developed into a branch banking system with such risks as existed spread not over a single community, or even a single region, but spread over the whole country. I believe this is preferable to the United States system of setting up independent local banks. The safety that springs from the system in use in this country is, of course, the justification for the branch banking system.
The Bank Act
The twofold responsibility assumed by the commercial bank manager is still regarded as being the principal responsibility today. However, changes in economic conditions have imposed upon the banking system a much wider responsibility to the public than heretofore was dreamed possible.
The great depression of the 1930's concentrated public attention-and I believe for the first time to any extent-upon the importance of the monetary system and its effect upon the general economy. It is now recognized that the banking system has a major responsibility in regulating the flow and direction of the nation's credit. That is why Canada, in common with many other countries, established a central bank; to give some over-all control over the system.
Now, the failure to provide proper credit regulation can be reflected of course in the fluctuation of prices, in the general condition of industry, in the condition of employment, in agricultural production and so on. In short, there can be general economic instability if there is failure to provide proper credit regulation.
Before the Bank of Canada was established the government could make advances, as the minister stated this afternoon, under the finance acts of 1914 and 1923, to the chartered banks in the form of Dominion of Canada notes against deposits made by the banks with the minister of finance. I think that is largely the genesis of our central banking system. Those deposits were in the form of securities approved by the minister and, as the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada said in their report issued in 1933-and I quote their words-it was entirely a matter "left to the discretion of the banks as to what their cash reserves would be" in relation to this.
The result was that they extended their bases of credit-and this caused a great deal of discussion in the early thirties-in periods of inflation and contracted them when depressed conditions should have demanded an increase in credit facilities. This was demonstrated very clearly in Canada between, we will say, 1925 and 1935, when for a few years we experienced a boom when credit was pretty easy, followed by a depression when things tightened up drastically. That concentrated public attention upon this problem probably to a greater extent than anything else could have done.
Today the regulation of the ratio between a bank's cash reserves and its deposits or liabilities is controlled by the Bank of Canada, and thus bank credit, the instrument which carries out, as we said the other day,

The Bank Act
the monetary policy, is largely laid down and controlled by the federal government. So it is no longer regarded as a matter of concern only to the individual bank in relation to its obligations to its depositors or to its own shareholders; it is now a matter of national interest.
Let me repeat what I said when I discussed the Bank of Canada Act the other day. The banking system has become, through the Bank of Canada operations, the instrument of monetary policy decided upon by the government. I want to repeat that. Yet, and here is the paradox, the actual financial decisions which affect public welfare are still in the hands of the private chartered banks. They decide how they shall meet demands for credit made upon them by various sectors of the economy, or indeed if the demand which is made upon them shall be met at all. The final decision is with the chartered banks, not with a public authority.
Because of the nature of the Canadian economy, consisting as it does so largely of primary and seasonal industries, the requirements for credit make the consideration of both short-term and intermediate-term credit a matter of primary concern, particularly to our primary industries. Take agriculture and fishing as examples. The farmer or the fisherman is dependent most of the time upon bank credit to carry him until he can realize on the sale of his products. That is particularly true of the farmer.
This kind of credit, or the issue of it, the granting of it, is entirely in the hands of the chartered banks and is a matter for their sole decision and judgment. Only in the larger industries which are able to finance out of their accumulated reserves is there less need to depend upon the chartered banks. I believe there is abundant evidence over the years to prove that in time of special need the chartered banks have failed to meet the important credit needs of agriculture and other seasonal and primary industries. Yet these are of fundamental importance to the Canadian economy.

speechtext:
He stated in his discussion of central banking in Canada, at page 124: The most distinctive feature of the Canadian system is the relatively small extent to which the Canadian banks engage in agricultural finance. They have customarily left the field of long and intermediate credit in rural districts almost entirely to other financial institutions, and have themselves' provided little but the seasonal needs of their rural clients.
I think that is equally true of fishermen. The fact of the matter is that farmers have succeeded in obtaining anything close to their short-term credit requirements only after government guarantees against losses have from time to time been given to the banks. That is the point I want to emphasize. This was recognized when the Farm Improvement Loans Act was passed in 1944 to provide short and intermediate credit for farm improvement and development. The act, we were told, was designed for the purpose of assisting "the average farmer who ordinarily would not be able to obtain bank credit for these purposes," and here I quote what was said at the time.
Under that act the government guaranteed losses up to 10 per cent of the total of the loans made by the banks. From the time the act became operative until December 1, 1952, the losses on those loans was only -01 per cent. That is to say, there was a loss of $1 for every $1,000 loaned under the act. I think that is a very impressive record. Thus the government guarantee of 10 per cent of the total loan meant that there was very little likelihood of the banks losing one cent under the act.
The other primary industry I mentioned was fishing. The fishermen have been unable to obtain short or intermediate-term credit, either from banks or from mortgage institutions, mainly because they lacked the necessary collateral.
In 1944, section 88 of the Bank Act, to which the minister referred this afternoon, authorized the banks to lend money upon the security of fishing vessels, fishing equipment and even the catch itself. But the authorization to lend under the act is one thing and the making of the loan or the securing of a loan is quite another thing. Parliament may authorize, but the banks make the final decision in what they conceive to be the interests of the banks and their shareholders rather than of the industry.

speechtext: And of the country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
And of the country. Mr. Ilsley, referring to the provision for such loans when it was brought up before the house, recognized this fact and I should like

to quote what he said, as reported on page 2560 of Hansard of 1944. He said that it would be necessary to-
-enact a companion measure somewhat similar to the Farm Improvement Loans Act-
I skip a few words.
-which will enable the government to give a limited guarantee in respect of loans made by chartered banks to fishermen.
He recognized that point. I do not know why, and I did not remember it until I began to prepare my notes for this discussion, but the suggestion of the minister of finance was never adopted by the house or by the government, with the result that the banks have not assumed the risk themselves of advancing necessary credit to this industry and the industry has had to go without necessary credit.
Generally speaking, these primary industries of farming and fishing have had to be assisted even in obtaining long-term credit through legislation and by government guarantees. The banks have not assumed the function which they should have assumed. I have in mind the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act, both administered by the Canadian farm loan board. I am not criticizing the banks in this latter respect with regard to long-term loans because they have been prohibited by law from lending on long-term mortgages, as the minister said this afternoon, ever since the first bank act was adopted by this parliament in 1871. What I have been referring to was their failure to provide the most essential intermediate and short-term credit when it was required.
Let me give a further illustration of the point I am making that only one type of pressure was used on the banks to make them accept even effective government guarantees against the losses which might have arisen when they agreed to meet certain important credit needs. The example I have in mind is the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act of 1937, which was passed when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and I were both new members in this house.
In 1944 the late Dr. Clark told the standing committee on banking and commerce, at the time of the last decennial revision, as reported at page 1366 of the proceedings, which I will summarize, that all the pressure possible had been used on the banks to make housing improvement loans and other loans to create employment, and that only because of this pressure did the banks make the loans that they would not normally have made.
It was clear from what Dr. Clark stated at that time that the banks yielded to this pressure because the act provided that the 83276-176i
The Bank Act
federal government would guarantee losses up to 10 per cent of the total amount of loans made by the banks. The banks incurred few if any losses, and such losses as did arise were covered by guarantees under the legislation. Dr. Clark's evidence can be found at page 1366 of the report of the committee's proceedings, and I would like to quote him directly from the record:
Our total losses up to date have been just a little over three-quarters of one per cent. I think the figure is -8 per cent. The loans are nearly all paid off. There is perhaps one or two million dollars of the principal still outstanding so even if all the rest of the loans were not recovered, if we did not recover a cent in respect of them, our total losses would be of the order of 2 or 2\ per cent, I believe. Actually we will recover a very substantial proportion of the amount of principal still outstanding so that the total loss ratio will be very low.
My purpose in referring to and reading this evidence is to show that without guarantees the banks would not advance credit to those people who were creditworthy, nor would they make loans to such people without specific government guarantees against loss.
We have often heard of private enterprise in connection with our banking system, but the banks required government guarantees against loss, thus eliminating the risks we are told the bankers take in making loans. Indeed, throughout the period under discussion at the moment the banks failed to meet the credit needs of the country or to take the risks they formerly undertook without guarantee.

As I said, however, I am not criticizing this feature. At one stage the government of Mr. R. B. Bennett, by means of a secret order in council-and the hon. member for Quebec South and the late minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, were both members of the opposition which dragged it into the open to the surprise of this house and the

country-allowed the banks, because of the position in which they had landed themselves in 1930, to value their securities at an unwarranted high level in order to prevent a run on one or two of the major banks. That was the value of the securities prior to a drastic drop in their value.

One outstanding example during the period to which I am referring was the $60 million loan made by eight chartered banks to the Canadian Pacific Railway in, I believe, 1933. Hon. members will recall the circumstances and will agree that this was done, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) I think will confirm, in order to prevent widespread unemployment at the Angus railway shops at Montreal and in other sectors in Canada. That entire loan was guaranteed by the federal government in 1933.
Again, because of the failure of our banking system in respect to certain phases of industrial development, this house had to take the initiative, and we passed an act placing the government in the banking business when we set up the industrial development bank. It was set up as a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada, which was authorized to buy the securities of the industrial development bank. Why was that done? The government explained very clearly at the time. chartered banks".

Yes, partly; but what I am getting at is that we saw fit to set up a bank

of our own to do what it was generally believed the banks were doing. Here was an admission that either the chartered banks were unable or were not permitted to fulfil the function for which they were brought into existence.
