speechtext:
-demonstrates that there was no justification for this particular move at all, if the banks functioned satisfactorily.
But I wish to pass on to another point. I want to suggest to the committee that there is another phase of this whole lending problem which should be given a thorough investigation, and I hope some means will be found of doing that. The banks have failed to meet the needs of the community; therefore we have small loan companies springing up all over Canada, opening up branches in almost every city and larger town in the country. They charge a rate of interest of 2 per cent per month. That is quite legal. They have been doing a huge business in Canada in the past few years. That indicates, I believe, that the chartered banks have not met the credit needs of the public.
One method of meeting the needs of the public would have been through credit unions, but unfortunately the spread of co-operative education and the organization of credit unions has so far failed to fill the gap. However, with more adequate educational efforts and encouragement on the part of governments, I think they could do so to a large extent.

In 1939 the Small Loans Act was passed. This act authorized small loan companies and personal money-lenders to make small and personal instalment loans "on the basis of a charge for interest and other costs of 2 per cent per month for loans extended up to 15 months". The reason the act was introduced, of course-and I say this immediately in fairness-was that it was necessary to regulate a widespread practice whereby money-lenders evaded existing laws relating to interest and usury. As early as 1936, however, one of the Canadian banks, namely the Canadian Bank of Commerce, organized a personal loan department to make loans to wage earners and others who could not qualify for such loans in the ordinary way of business. I often think that if the Bank of Commerce or the other chartered banks doing this sort of business would publicize to a greater extent the facilities they offer, many people who now go to these loan sharks and pay 2 per cent per month would be able to get some help at least from the banks, although the banks do not meet the need that exists.
What was the experience of this new department of the Canadian Bank of Commerce? Mr. Stewart, the assistant general manager of the bank, appeared before the banking and commerce committee in 1944. He showed that loans were made at, I think, an effective interest rate of about 11-78 per cent. Again, the hon. minister's predecessor, Mr. Ilsley, proposed an amendment to the Bank Act to regularize these bank loans with an effective interest rate not to exceed 9| per cent. That proposal was dropped. I think it would be well for the committee to question the banks carefully as to their experience with loans of this description, particularly with a view to curtailing or, better still, eliminating the operations of the small loan companies with their extortionate if legal rate of interest. It might inquire into that matter, for I do not remember why the proposal Mr. Ilsley brought in for an effective rate of interest of 9f per cent was dropped. I do not remember it, and I could not find the reason for dropping it in my search of the records.
The committee should also consider how the rapid development of credit unions could be promoted, because they operate in a quite different way. They operate among people whom they know and to those who need them they are able to provide loans more on the basis of personal integrity and character than on the possession of collateral which the banks and indeed the loan companies demand. Under a branch banking system I suppose the branch managers are obliged to do this.
The Bank Act
Hon. members might look at page 300 of the report of the last banking and commerce committee. I was going to make some quotations from it but I cannot do that. There they will find a fairly complete record of the operations of the personal loan department of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. In the first seven and a half years of operation- that is, up to 1944-Mr. Stewart testified that only one-quarter of one per cent of the loans had to be repaid by the guarantors of personal loans made by the Canadian Bank of Commerce. I believe that bank required two guarantors in connection with these loans. From the reading of the evidence it would appear that up to that time at least the bank really lost nothing under the arrangement.
That the banks are unwilling to extend credit facilities to meet national problems was clearly stated again recently by Mr. T. H. Atkinson, president of the Canadian Bankers Association, before the banking and commerce committee when it was discussing the housing bill to which we gave third reading this afternoon. He replied to a question relating to the financing of housing in these words:
Such a move would not. I think, have been sought by the banks-particularly at the present time when the chartered banks in Canada are relatively "fully loaned".
If time permits, I should like to say a little bit later something about that statement to the effect that the banks are fully loaned. In his capacity as general manager of the Royal Bank he added, "Certainly in our own case it would not".
I am not going into the question of housing finance under the proposed new housing act, but it should be noted that bank credit facilities to meet this public need are only being reluctantly extended in consideration of the banks receiving ironclad guarantees against any losses under this act. Why is it that the banks have never made any serious effort to meet outstanding credit needs of the country? First, the banks have always raised the question of liquidity when it has been suggested that they are not fulfilling their obligation to the nation. In other words this objection underlines the conflict, which I noted in the discussion of the Bank of Canada Act, between on the one hand the private banks and their admitted obligations to the depositors-shareholders and, on the other hand, what I conceive to be the obligations of the banking system to the public as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, lest I forget or go over my time a moment or two, I am going to move now the amendment that we have in mind. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That Bill No. 338 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the national ownership and public control of the chartered banks.
Before dinner I was remarking that there appeared to be a conflict between the interests of the public and the interests of the banks when we consider the matter of making loans and providing the necessary credit to the community. Of course it would be foolish for me or for anyone else to deny that there is some validity in the argument that the banks must be in a position at all times to fulfil the demands of their depositors for the withdrawal of their funds immediately or on short notice. The banks must have liquid reserves sufficient to meet such demands whenever they arise. However, the liquidity of the banks has for a long time exceeded anything the most conservative banker of other times ever anticipated.
The reason for this is the long-term decline in the relative importance of bank lending. It is only in the last few years that some recovery has been made, but the ratio of bank loans to total bank assets is still far lower than it was in the earlier part of this century. I say that statement is beyond dispute, as I think I can show.
Today bank loans constitute as little as 35 per cent of total bank assets, while before the first world war bank loans constituted over 60 per cent of total bank assets. This is confirmed by the monthly review of the Bank of Nova Scotia in its September and October, 1953, issues. In the latest annual report of the Royal Bank of Canada the general manager, Mr. Atkinson, after analysing their call loans, government and municipal bonds and holdings of other securities, together with cash on hand, had this to say:
This amount represents what is normally referred to as the liquid assets of the bank and equals 65-42 per cent of the bank's liabilities to the public.
But even this does not tell the whole story of the Royal Bank's liquid position-I selected the Royal Bank only because its general
[Mr. Coldwell. 1
manager appeared before the committee the other day-for it has in addition a reserve fund of $70 million which is twice as large as its total paid-up capital. Then, of course, before net profits are declared appropriations are made by the banks to cover their so-called contingencies. These can be used against bad or doubtful debts and to provide additional working capital for the bank.
Of course it would be absurd even to discuss this matter except that the banks' liquidity is always raised when they are required to undertake certain lending activities. If a bank finds itself embarrassed it can of course always fall back on the rediscounting facilities provided by parliament through the Bank of Canada. The fact that these facilities have very seldom been used is additional proof of the excellent liquid position of the chartered banks.
Throughout the war bank investments in government securities were unusually high. This was because they were used to assist our financing of the war. Since the war bank holdings of government securities have declined. It is difficult, however, to reconcile the facts of the case with Mr. Atkinson's statement that the banks are "fully loaned". I am not naive enough to expect that privately-owned banks will meet all the public needs which I have discussed, when they consider that their own interests must be their first consideration.
The banks are profit-motivated institutions. Their lending activities and investments, if they coincide with the public welfare, do so rather by accident than by deliberate planning. If it is more profitable and safer to invest in government securities than it is to undertake loans to fishermen, farmers or individual Canadians, then the banks will invest in government securities.
Let us take a look at their net profits for a moment. Their net profits indicate that they have followed principles in accordance with their business instincts. In 1945 the net profits of the Canadian banks were $12,541,408. By 1950 they had risen to $23,429,363. In 1951 there was a slight decline to $22,743,225, but in 1953 they had risen again to $30,386,000.

speechtext:
No, after. I was about to say that it should be noted that these profits are after full provision has been made for contingency reserves, depreciation and income tax. If we take their percentage of net profits to their paid-up capital, according to the latest figures, which were placed on Hansard last Friday, I believe, we find that the percentage of net profits to the paid-up

capital of the three largest Canadian banks, the Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal and the Canadian Bank of Commerce in 1953 was 24-67 per cent, 19-56 per cent and 19-30 per cent respectively.
The point of my argument is this, that as long as the banks continue to be privately owned their managing officers must inevitably and quite properly continue to give priority to their obligations to their shareholders rather than to the credit needs of the Canadian people. This is the paradoxical position of our banking system. It is expected on the one hand to regulate and provide money and credit to maintain the economic welfare of the nation, and on the other hand its obligations to its shareholders demand that it be operated with the object of producing the highest possible profits. We believe this conflict can only be resolved by bringing the banking system under public ownership. Let me quote from a memorandum submitted to the banking and commerce committee in 1944 by the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section. They said:
We consider that as the money and credit system of Canada is actually the heart which must regularly and evenly pulsate to keep the economic body properly functioning, it is therefore too important to the very life and well-being of the nation to be entrusted to private corporations.
Of course it was said this afternoon that a publicly-owned system would perhaps lead to political interference. I think one of my colleagues may discuss, either here or in the banking and commerce committee, the record of that great publicly-owned institution in the Commonwealth of Australia, the Commonwealth Bank, one of the great commercial and now central banks of the world today.
May I conclude by summarizing the concessions the banks have received over the years in order to show that the risk has been taken out of banking, that wherever there was risk the government stepped in and guaranteed them against that risk. First of all we have the finance acts of 1914 and 1923. That was the beginning. They allowed the banks to obtain dominion notes against deposits of their securities with the finance minister. Then of course there was the very valuable privilege allowing them to create all the credits they cared to create without limitation, until the Bank of Canada was established in 1935.
In 1933, as I remarked this afternoon, we had the C.P.R. loan of $60 million by eight banks which was guaranteed in full by order in council. This afternoon I mentioned the fact that when the banks were in a difficult position in the early 1930's another and secret
The Bank Act
order in council was passed so that the real position of one or two of the banks at least would not be known to the Canadian people.
I am not saying I am critical of that, because had there been a run on those banks there might have been something of a financial panic in the country. In 1937 we had the Home Improvement Loans Guarantee Act, under which loans were guaranteed up to 10 per cent of the total loans made. In 1944 there was the farm loans act which guaranteed against losses up to 10 per cent of the total loans.
May I just remark, because I did not do so this afternoon when I was mentioning this, that it was suggested, as I recall it, by Mr. Ilsley that we should have a fisherman's loan act somewhat similar. I had forgotten that the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) made a similar proposal in May, I think it was, of last year. This year again, 1954, we have the housing act under which we guarantee 98 per cent of the loans and the provision that the banks can sell their mortgages to the central bank, and I think they hope to sell some housing mortgages to the public. I recall that in 1944, though I could not put my hand on the quotation, Mr. Graham Towers told the banking and commerce committee that in his 25 years of experience in banking, which covered the depression period, the losses of the banks were not more than f of 1 per cent. If my recollection does not play me false he also remarked he had heard bankers say that over the period of Canadian banking the losses of the banks would not be more than j of 1 per cent.
My point is this. We guarantee the banks against losses: we eliminate their risks; we allow them to take all the profits that are in the banking business, and we in this parliament take all the risks. Where is there private enterprise in a banking system of that description? Is it not time we took the profits for the people of Canada as well as the risks?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at once that we will not be able to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), chiefly because we feel that it is not in the best interests of the country to nationalize the banks.
When I spoke at the committee stage of this bill I believe I said that I never did take very seriously those declarations that are frequently made that such and such a party would nationalize the banks. The fact is we have heard declarations of that kind for many years in many places. The socialist party have been famous for saying that they would nationalize the chartered banks. They

The Bank Act
got themselves in a position to do so in Britain, and backed away from it. They got themselves in a position to do so in Australia, and backed clear away from it. I do not know any place where they have done so.
All down the years, as a matter of fact, so far as I can recall, they have been among the chief supporters of the system of finance that has controlled the banking system, which in turn has controlled the industrial system, in the various countries. The hon. member mentioned the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and stated that during the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee one of his colleagues would outline the great record of that institution. Well, everyone knows that is not a chartered bank but a central bank. We have one, too.

speechtext:
It is not to be compared with the chartered banks of this country. There would have to be more than a delineation of the record of the Commonwealth Bank to prove that nationalization of the banks would be in the interests of the people.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, what difference would nationalization make? It is not the ownership of the bank that counts but the policy that is followed. In this country we have what is purported to be public control of the chartered banks; that is why the Bank of Canada was set up in 1934. Through it can be exercised any amount of public control to which the government is prepared to agree. The whole thing resolves itself down to a question of government policy, and how far that policy is prepared to go in the control of currency and credit.
I am much more concerned about government policy than I am about the ownership of the banks. Let me say, though, that if at any time the government laid down a specific, comprehensive policy for the control of currency and credit in the public interest, and the chartered banks refused to cooperate in the administration of that policy, then of course it might be necessary to consider nationalization. I cannot imagine that situation would ever arise in Canada. Until it does, then I would not take very seriously the question of nationalization of the banks.
The legislation now before parliament is of greater importance to the Canadian people, in our judgment, than almost any legislation that is ever brought before us. Because they

touch so intimately the lives and interests of every Canadian; because the welfare, the security and freedoms of all our people depend so much upon what is provided in the Bank Act and its companion piece the Bank of Canada Act, I believe every member of this house should be sufficiently interested to make a thorough and detailed study of the acts themselves as well as of banking practices and procedure. A thorough study should be made of government financial and economic policy, which must go along with those acts.
Now, those three things, the Bank Act, the Bank of Canada Act and government financial policy, are so closely related, in my judgment, they cannot be separated in any attempt to study the impact of finance upon the Canadian economy and upon the lives and fortunes of our people. I suggest that the success of our work in connection with these important measures this year will depend to a great extent on our approach to them. We shall not get far, nor will we do much of a job for the people who sent us here, if we take for granted that finance is a mystery that no layman can understand, or if we are too ready to believe that we have a perfect banking system.
Let me say right here that I believe we have a strong banking system, and an efficient one and a good one. If we believe for one moment, however, it is perfect we are not going to do much of a job in connection with the consideration of the Bank Act. If we believe that Adam Smith and John Stuart Mill, and perhaps other economists, enunciated immutable economic laws with which our banking and financial policies are in complete harmony, we shall get no place. We are likely to get some place if we approach our studies of these two bills with the assurance that finance is no mystery, except as it is made to appear so by those pundits. If we approach the study believing that there are weaknesses in our banking system that have to be corrected, and if we approach our study from the point of view that the economic laws enunciated by Adam Smith and John Stuart Mill are only economic practices and conventions operating in certain periods of economic development, which are being constantly outmoded by the march of events and the tempo of human progress, then we shall get some place.
Now, when the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act are before the banking and commerce committee we intend to give them the most searching study of which we are capable, and a full inquiry, no matter how long it may take. I do not wish to go deeply into the history of banking at this time, but I have

a purpose in wanting to make a very brief, historical statement of the reasons we Social Crediters are so deeply interested in the subject of finance and banks.
The industrial revolution brought about great struggles between nations for markets. During these struggles the internal economies of the nations involved were undergoing tremendous change. The individual industrialists began to find that unrestricted competition among themselves was often a form of business suicide. It was better, they thought, to avoid such competition by amalgamating their common interests, and so monopolies were born. This, in turn, demanded larger and ever larger issues of capital and evergrowing recourse to overdrafts with the banks for working expenses.
The powers of the banks which alone had the right to create financial credit grew rapidly with this change in the internal economy, and became the dominating factor in business everywhere. Industrial capitalism gave way to finance capitalism, and this is now universal in all democratic countries.
It was recognized quite early by great financiers and bankers that the control of industry and of the nation itself resided in the banking system, and that the power of creating, regulating and controlling bank credit made them, in a way, a hidden government, practically overriding and controlling every activity of the national life.
This great fact, with its wide implications and effects, was kept as secret as possible from the public for many years and was, for quite obvious reasons, denied by the banks themselves. Most economists and politicians do not seem to have discovered it to this day. And, except for monetary reformers, -and we include ourselves in monetary reformers-it is still more or less a secret.
With the growth of trade between nations and the need for adjusting the necessary means of exchange, banking became international in its operations, and the great banks of the world became related organizations, functioning to their mutual advantage. This international co-operation of the banks had a parallel influence on the monopolies they controlled through overdrafts and interlocking directorates. These industrial monopolies became international also, and are one of the features of today-the giant cartels and combines appearing in the industries of all countries, and of course levying tribute in peace and war from both friend and enemy.
Canada is within the ambit of these industrial and financial forces, and it seems to me we would be very blind if we did not see these operations around us everywhere. The 8327&-177
The Bank Act
system I have been describing is often spoken of as the system of private enterprise or capitalism.
This is not, of course, the place to discuss the merits and demerits of the system. But arising out of it are certain manifestations that cannot be disregarded by any red-blooded man who is anxious for the welfare and future of his country. The disparity between the great wealth of the industrial capitalists and the appalling poverty among all the workers in the industrial system some years ago became quite obvious to a large number of people, and gave rise to bitter and, I suppose, in a measure justifiable discontent.
Exploitation of men, women and children in the early stages of the industrial period makes one of the blackest pages in history. No one can read history without being convinced of that. From the humanitarian point of view the system known in that day as capitalism-and I am speaking of the day of the industrial revolution-stood condemned, and there was much revolt against its economic effects on a large proportion of the people.
Out of the revolt that took place against it arose the trade union movement in Great Britain, the regulation of child labour, the factory acts, the fixing of hours and wages and, on the intellectual side, the theories of socialism and the gospel of Karl Marx. These interests got into war with one another, and they have never been reconciled to this day. So even now we stand in a world of economic conflict in which the contending forces of capitalism and communism are striving for mastery.
From the Social Credit point of view it would be tragedy for either side to conquer. We believe that salvation for human beings lies along the middle road that we are following, the road to Social Credit. That is our deep conviction, when we realize that the age of abundance has in reality arrived, providing plenty for everybody. We know that we can have economic security with freedom, which is the first step along the road to the new era of abundance which we seek. We can secure that first step, not by revolution and force but by a new financial concept, the central point of which is making money and credit the true reflection of material facts, and using them and controlling them for the benefit of the whole community.
Now, we think nothing-and I am speaking generally of people in this day-of controlling public utilities such as the supply of gas, the milk supply, electricity, railroads,

The Bank Act
and all that sort of thing. We never think of dictatorship or slavery or anything of that kind when we lay down laws and policies to control these things. People today justify themselves by saying that these things touch the lives of the people so closely and affect them so intimately that they have to be controlled in the interests of all the people.
Well, I ask hon. members, what greater utility is there than the supply of money and credit? But when some of us advocate nonpolitical money management in the interests of all the people in the country, there are certain people who jump at the chance to charge us with wanting dictatorship. Actually what we want to do is relieve the people from the great dictatorship under which they have suffered for years.
Sometimes the term "money management" is misunderstood

and I am saying this for the benefit of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). He is a good friend of mine, whose opinion I respect. But I say that sometimes the term "money management" is misunderstood, and perhaps in some quarters deliberately so. I will not say that in connection with the hon. member, because I believe he really believes what he says. I wish to pay him that compliment. However, in order to illustrate what I mean let me point out that Abraham Lincoln is credited with having made this statement:
The government should create, issue and circulate all the currency and credit needed to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers. This is the government's greatest creative opportunity.
In that quotation from Lincoln the word "government" needs some amplification. It is not necessary-in fact it may not even be desirable-that government, in the narrow sense of that word, should do the regulating. The point, so far as we Social Crediters view it, is that it must be done by a responsible body of men on the strength of accurate federal statistical information, and it must not be left to chance.
It does not matter, as I say, whether it is done by this body or by that body, so long as it is a responsible body of men. And that could mean the government. It could be carried out by the Bank of Canada, by a special committee appointed by industry, agriculture, banking and government known as, let us say, a permanent monetary commission; or it could even be done by a national banking association under a policy carefully and specifically laid down for it by the government. And in all those cases it would be government-controlled, as we view it.
When it is said that such a task allotted to the government would give it too great

powers and perhaps admit of too much political interference, I say that is not true, especially when it is reviewed in the light of the explanation I have just given. The government has greater and more dangerous powers today than that, by far. And for all practical purposes the government can raise all the money it finds necessary for its activities at the present time, mainly by expropriating it through taxation. It can do that through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
Surely that is not to be compared with what we have suggested by way of money management. Under the Social Credit proposals, even if the powers were allotted to the government in its narrowest sense-the government being those on the front benches over here, of whom my genial friend the Minister of Finance is a leading member- it would be allowed to create money only corresponding to the power of production, which at any time can be determined with about 90 per cent accuracy by our bureau of statistics.
Whether Abraham Lincoln realized fully the implication of his words I do not know, but they mean in terms of our present sciences that the sum total of money creation must not surpass the sum strictly needed to ensure buying the goods that may be produced and are wanted at any given time. The spending power of the government and the buying power of the consumer strictly limit the powers of government if they take the controlling power. Anything in excess of that would mean inflation. On the other hand, insufficiency would mean deflation and eventual depression and starvation which would require a war to get out of. We do not want that sort of thing.
The bill we are considering is not merely a simple amending bill; it is a revision of the whole Bank Act. Consequently there are many clauses which relate to routine matters of procedure to which I suppose we will not pay too much attention because they have been in operation for many years and have proved to operate and function smoothly. However, there are a few sections which are of particular concern and interest to the country at this time. Mr. Speaker, I hasten to assure you that I am not going to deal with specific sections, except to name the clause and speak of the principle.
Section 75 provides authority for the chartered banks to make loans in connection with housing on the security of insured mortgages. The government expects the banks to put up a good share of the mortgage money which the government has put up in recent

years under the joint loan arrangements with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As far as I can tell, the banks are not enthusiastic about this authority. Unless they become more socially-minded than they appear to be at the present time they will not be making up the 25 per cent of the mortgage money which the government put up last year. That is my guess. They may do it, and if they do I shall be the first to compliment them. But from what I have seen I would not think that will happen.
There must be additional cash reserves provided to the banks if they are to be able to make any reasonable contribution to housing in the years ahead. How are those cash reserves to be provided? We have suggested already to the banking and commerce committee the way in which those reserves can be provided, and at the same time a fund for low-income housing by which municipalities could service land for housing and build houses at an interest rate of from 2 to 3 per cent. This could be done under some such arrangement as the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. The only argument against our proposal that we have heard thus far is that it was not government policy. We knew that, but we would like to have someone come to grips with it and show why it would not be good government policy.
Section 82 of the Bank Act authorizes the banks to make loans to oil companies for oil development, taking various kinds of securities including the security of the oil pool away down under the earth. That is quite a departure. In my judgment this provision will go a long way to help oil development in the prairie provinces. I think it is a splendid idea. I wonder why it was not done long before. I had thought it might be due to the fact that we were finding it difficult to get working capital in some places. In my judgment this provision will be of great help.
In the past oil companies with the most excellent prospects have been forced to seek capital in the United States or some other country because of a lack of operating credit here. There has been altogether too much of that sort of thing, but it was inevitable if development were to take place. We should be supplying much more of our own capital for Canadian development-just as much as we possibly can, as a matter of fact. Otherwise foreign control begins to extend itself, and in my judgment that is not good for the country. In fact it contains elements of danger. For that reason among others we welcome this particular change in the Bank Act.
The Bank Act
Clause 6 provides for a revision of the Bank Act in 1964. Somehow or other we have got into the habit of thinking that the act should not come before parliament oftener than every ten years. That was answered only partially today when it was said that the balance should be established between stability on the one hand, I think the minister said, and flexibility on the other. I agree that that is desirable, but I cannot see that there is any connection between that desirable balance and having the Bank Act come up for revision only every ten years. I doubt that there is. It is just that we have got in the habit of thinking there is. I think that ten years, which covers the life of almost three parliaments, is too long. Just think of it, it covers most of the life of three parliaments. If we continue with our present practice of a decennial revision, the idea is bound to grow up that the Bank Act and our financial policy are somewhat sacrosanct, or untouchable. I am afraid there is that feeling now in some quarters.
We suggest that the annual statements of the chartered banks and the annual report of the Bank of Canada be referred to the banking and commerce committee at least once during each parliament, and that on each of those occasions a complete review be made before that committee by the governor of the Bank of Canada. In my judgment such a procedure would bring parliament in much closer touch with financial policy than has been the case in the past. I believe the more you think of that suggestion the more it will appeal to your judgment.
At the same time we also press for the setting up of a committee similar to the reconstruction committee which was established by parliament about ten years ago. That reconstruction committee did a good job, and some of its recommendations have been approved by the government. If it were reconstituted it could make an annual or biennial review of the economic situation in Canada. It could make recommendations to parliament, and those recommendations could be related closely to the financial considerations and recommendations of the banking and commerce committee. I believe those are things which we should think of.
Perhaps a most far-reaching change in the Bank Act is made in section 71, which introduces the variable reserve principle. This section must be considered in conjunction with section 18 (1) (o) of the Bank of Canada Act. Section 71 of the bill now before us specifies a floor of 8 per cent on cash reserve requirements, but it does not specify a ceiling. That is interesting. The Bank of Canada Act sets a ceiling at 12 per cent.
83276-177J

The Bank Act
We believe that this variability of cash reserve requirements is a step in the right direction, but we think the act should provide for a much higher ceiling. Not that we think we should jump immediately to a much higher cash reserve requirement, not at all; but if the mechanism is there it will prove mighty useful when it is needed. We think that by so doing the Bank of Canada can provide purchasing power to the government of the country with which the government can buy new business activities for the country when they are needed, business activities in the form of housing, highways or slum-pardon me, I must not say "slum clearance" since last week -for substandard housing clearance and so on, to the extent that ordinary commercial channels do not keep economic activities at the highest possible level.
Those who have studied this idea know that such a provision of purchasing power to the government by the Bank of Canada would mean no additional expense to the nation at all. On the contrary, it would save expenses, and particularly taxes.
The two acts now before parliament, taken together and viewed in the light of government policy, have, in my judgment, two serious weaknesses. The first of these is that government policy continues to accept the fallacy that for the goods produced somehow or somewhere enough purchasing power will be brought into existence which will enable these goods to reach the hands of the consumers. But that just is not so. That is a delusion. Under our wages system of distribution of purchasing power, and under the peculiar way in which we finance capital development and expansion, a shortage of purchasing power is always generated in times of peace. It may not occur in times of war because then we give away the top third or approximately 40 per cent of what we produce. It is largely because of the failure of our present system to distribute mass-consumer purchasing power in sufficient quantities to make it possible for people to buy back what they produce that periodically we find our country as a whole with what we call large surpluses of production with consequent unemployment, recession and possibly depression.
There are many authorities today to testify to the truth of that statement. I shall not spend time quoting all of them, but I would like to quote one who spent 18 years as head of the economics department of one of the great universities in the United States,

the University of Texas. At page 33 of his book "The Divine Right of Capital" he said, speaking of our economy:
It fails to distribute mass-consumer purchasing power in sufficient quantity to permit the entire product of industry to be purchased. This failure exists at all times under capitalism and is noxious at all times.
That is a quotation from Professor C. E. Ayres, who as I have already said was head of the economics department of the University of Texas. He is only one of many who have testified to the shortage of purchasing power generated under our present system, and if we look around and take cognizance of our economic history we will observe over the years a succession of booms and slumps in times of peace which, in time of war, disappear because we are giving away the top third of all our products. Perhaps instead of saying it has disappeared I should say it is negatived, because it is generated in wartime as well as in peacetime although we do not see it in wartime because we give away part of that production.
When we go into a slump the one way to get out of it short of war is to increase the mass-consumer purchasing power in the country. No other factor will accomplish this task, as far as I can see. There cannot possibly be real security with freedom for all our people, no matter how great our Canadian productive capacity may become, unless and until government financial policy recognizes the shortage of purchasing power generated under our present system of distributing that purchasing power and financing plant expansion and renewal of heavy industry.
Before I deal with the second weakness to which I have referred I would like to say a word about the minister's speech this afternoon. I wish to thank him for the attention he obviously paid to what I said on March 4. The minister observed that while he did not agree with the emphasis I placed on fiscal means, yet he found what I said of some interest. I thank the minister for that. Perhaps I did not make myself quite clear the other day, but I certainly meant at any rate to recognize, and I do recognize, a number of non-monetary factors as well as monetary ones which do have an effect upon our economy. I believe the one factor which to some degree influences all the other factors is the regulation of the volume of deposit money. As I said during that speech on March 4, and I quote from page 2556 of Hansard:
Of late years many outstanding authorities have come to believe that eight of these factors can be influenced by regulating the volume of deposit

money In this country. The chartered banks are almost if not completely in control of deposit money. It is within their sole discretion to grant or refuse loans, which is the means, of course, by which deposit money is brought into existence.
I believe that is what the minister is referring to, and I quite agree with him. I would like it definitely known here that I recognize there are non-monetary factors which affect our economy, and there are certainly monetary factors which also affect the economy. I believe the minister will agree with me that the one which exercises some influence over all the others is the regulation of the cash reserves of the chartered banks which, of course, regulate in turn the volume of deposit money.
I placed emphasis on one of these factors while at the same time recognizing that there are others. I would like the minister to note that I believe perhaps one of the most important of the non-fiscal means of affecting our economy is taxation, which does have a profound effect on the economy. There are things he could accomplish by lowering taxes which could perhaps be accomplished just as well by increasing the volume of purchasing power.
Let me deal with the second weakness to which I referred in the government's financial policy. This second weakness is one which I mentioned at the committee stage of the resolution. I refer to the lack of an efficient mechanism by which the government and the Bank of Canada can quickly and successfully halt at the point of equilibrium a deflationary operation brought on by the Bank of Canada when it uses its powers to decrease the cash reserves of the chartered banks.
I hope that when we get into committee the minister will join hands with the governor of the Bank of Canada and permit us to examine that point. I do not believe they have the answer, nor do I believe they have the mechanism, and I am satisfied in my own mind that when the cash reserves are decreased as a means of halting an inflationary tendency or an inflation, then the banks must reduce their deposit liabilities by calling in loans. When the downward trend is started it is like a chain reaction carried along by its own momentum. It will not stop itself short of recession or depression, unless some way is provided of quickly putting purchasing power into the hands of consumers so they can put on the brakes and ease off the accelerator by buying the surpluses of available goods and taking them off the market.
That is the only way I can see of doing it, and the minister has not shown me that there is an alternative brake to halt the
The Bank Act
downward movement. A softening up or lending policy will not do the job, because no bank will be prepared to make loans to producers to produce more of the things which already cannot be sold. A deflationary movement makes the borrowers uncreditworthy, when before they have been looked upon as good risks. What is needed is a means by which the Bank of Canada can make available to the government enough credit to balance the effective demand with the available goods and services in the country to make up the deficiency of purchasing power and to halt the downward trend.
A start in the direction of getting such a mechanism was made when the variable reserve principle was injected into the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act. The government could use that principle to make it possible for the Bank of Canada to provide the government with national credits on the basis of government deposit certificates lodged, with the bank. But if such a thing is to be of real value, the ceiling on cash reserve requirements will have to be raised considerably above the 12 per cent limit imposed by paragraph (o) of subsection 1 of section 18 of the Bank of Canada Act.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker-I see that my time has elapsed-may I say that our concern in connection with financial policy is that every possible scientific fiscal means be included in our government's policy to ensure freedom from inflation on the one hand and freedom from depression or recession on the other. We are anxious about the lack of an effective brake and accelerator in the government's money management machinery. We want the optimum development of our country's resources and the most equitable possible distribution of the goods and services that our country can produce.
When the bills are before the committee we shall put forward specific proposals that will strengthen our financial policy and make it effective in insulating our country against inflation, and in guaranteeing our people economic security with freedom.

speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. I thought there were to be several other speakers. I had no idea that the debate would reach this stage so soon. Perhaps it is a good thing, and shows what an admirable presentation the minister made today.
There are, however, one or two points I should like to mention about what he said today, and I think I had better start off with this one. I was not able to hear the entire speech of the leader of the C.C.F. group, but in reply to the plea for nationalization of the banks, I think I should first of all say that the banks are the people. I do not know how many millions of people are depositors in the banks today, but a huge majority of the Canadian people are depositors in and Users of the banks. Not only that, but the banks through their shareholders are owned by a great number of Canadians across Canada, the average shareholder having only comparatively few shares. Therefore I think one of the great assets in our Canadian banking system is that it is used by a large number of Canadians, who own it either through deposits or through their ownership of shares. It is a truly national system now.
The minister today made a point having to do with the alteration of the type of bank share. I do not know whether or not the banks are going to accept that alteration, but I want to make this suggestion. At the present time the banks have what is known as book stock. The stock is, as the name implies, only transferrable on the books of the various chartered banks. It is not good collateral at the banks. I think that is a useful quality of bank stock. I say this because, during the depression, one of the types of security which maintained its price, its equity and its income better than any except gold shares was bank stock. One

of the banks-I think it was the Bank of Toronto-in its annual report after the depression made a special point of saying how few shareholders of the bank had to liquidate their stocks for various reasons.
I think the fact that the bank stocks today are not good collateral is one of their most valuable features. I would hate to see the bank stocks become negotiable securities, like common stock certificates. If the bank issues scrip stock which is transferable merely by signing on the back, and which can be used as collateral either to protect a broker's loan or to protect a loan at the bank, it becomes like any other stock. Human nature being what it is, I am afraid that when a loan needs more collateral or a broker needs more margin, it is only natural to put up the good stocks. Then if things go from bad to worse the real assets will be lost. I think that was one of the great assets of our type of bank stocks during the depression.
In the bill I notice that there is nothing to suggest that a savings bank or any type of corporation such as the savings and loans associations in the United States are contemplated. I am not a professional banker, but certainly the savings and loans associations in the United States, together with the mutual savings banks, have assets of some $43 billion dollars, which represents about half the time deposits in the United States-a useful source of mortgage money, to say the least. The figure for demand loans in the United States at November 25, 1953 was $100 billion and for time loans $69 billion. Of that $69 billion, about $43 billion was in the form of assets of savings banks and trust and loans associations. As I say, I am not putting forward my opinion that this is something that should be in the act, but I certainly feel that here is an opportunity for study with a view to the raising of funds for real estate mortgages and other purposes under the housing act we have just passed.
There is one other point I should like to bring out. The banks are to be asked to provide funds for housing loans. The evidence we have had shows that their reluctance is not based on the use of their capital, assets and deposits, but is based on a lack of knowledge of the housing and mortgage business. They are afraid of being forced into a business which up to this time has been specifically proscribed by the act, and now they find that the situation is turned about and they are being put directly into the mortgage business. It is my opinion that possibly the banks will want to form an organization which will act for the chartered

banks as a group, so that instead of having eleven mortgage and loan associations there will be one association which will do the actual technical work of providing mortgages, servicing loans and performing the other work which is not done by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the present time.
When the bill goes to the committee I hope, if the banks should consider it desirable to enter into such an arrangement, some agreement can be reached so the banks will not be contravening the combines act. Here we have an entirely new situation, one in which the banks may really wish to co-operate. Because of their lack of knowledge of the mortgage business they will be hesitant to embark upon the lending of money on mortgages. The evidence before the banking and commerce committee showed very clearly that it is not a case of unwillingness to act on the part of the banks, but rather a lack of knowledge that inhibits them at the present time.
I would also hope that in the not too distant future the banks will again be allowed to have gold as part of their assets. I believe that the right of our chartered and commercial banks to use gold as part of their reserves should be restored to them. I feel that the issuing of gold certificates by the chartered banks could be a very useful form of assistance in facilitating international trade.
I merely make these few suggestions because I do not want to hold up the bill, and because they were not mentioned by the minister when he introduced the measure this afternoon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose there are very few subjects, with the possible exception of the sort of witchcraft upon which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) frowns, that are surrounded with quite so much mythology and superstition as the subject we are discussing tonight. I have always been entertained to note that only within the last 20 or 30 years those who are in control of the temples of finance have been prepared to admit truths that were enunciated almost 300 years ago by, as one would guess, a gentleman of the same racial origin as myself. He was the father of modern banking, a man called Paterson, who sold a very smart idea to King William III in Great Britain when, in return for the privilege of issuing the then newly developing paper currency, he provided King William III with funds to fight some of his continental wars. Mr. Paterson had no illusions at all about the sort of business he was engaged in or about the realities of that business, but it is only within comparatively
The Bank Act
recent years that we have had fairly clear recognition of these same principles on which Mr. Paterson worked 300 years ago.
I was very interested in reading not long ago a book by the eminent Australian economist, L. F. Giblin, on the affairs of the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Professor Giblin has some rather satirical comments to make on the curious myths and illusions which those who were in charge of banking and financial matters in Australia about 30 years ago held with regard to the realities of their business. I noted in this book that it took experience to convince those gentlemen that they were really living in a world in which the basis of a financial system is trust and confidence, shall we say, rather than a more solid, metallic basis. These myths and folklores of course have been very useful to those who control the financial system, just as the myths and folklores of the old priests of Egypt used to delude the people of that country.
Earlier today the leader of this group gave an account of the very profitable operations of the chartered banks of Canada, and I do not believe I need to go into that. I do not think, at any rate, that the actual fact of the really exorbitant profits, and they are exorbitant, which the chartered banks of Canada have made over the years is a very important point. I think the important point made by the leader of this group was that the government had repeatedly not merely come to the rescue of the banks but had been obliged to protect the banking system of this country by legislation from every possibility of danger and disaster-and quite rightly, too. It is important to us that the financial system of the country should operate smoothly and efficiently, without danger of breakdowns, just as it is that our transmission lines should continue to supply electric power and that our water mains should supply water for the consumption of the urban population. As I say, it was quite necessary that they should do so.
However, that raises this point, Mr. Speaker. A sector of our economy that is so essential that our government must at all costs make sure there shall be no shadow of danger attending its operations is far too important to be left in private hands. In fact it seems to me there is no moral justification for leaving in private hands a sector of the economy that must at all times be supported by the people and by the government of this country; which must be rescued if at any time it has taken some injudicious action, and that must always be, in the final resort, able to come back on the government of Canada. I believe

The Bank Act
that is the first point we should bear in mind in considering the proposals made by this group for the public ownership of the banking system.
Only today in this chamber we concluded the discussion of a piece of legislation that is an example of the government's inability to direct the operations of our financial system in the way in which this government considers it should be directed for the welfare of the people of Canada. There can be no doubt that the government takes the position, and quite rightly, that housing is an important matter to the Canadian people. It requires the investment of the savings of the Canadian people to provide that housing. We have to hold out inducements, and hope that the people who own this particular sector of our economy will co-operate with us and do what we, as the people's representatives, consider should be done with the savings of the people of Canada. We have no guarantee that they are going to do it. In fact there is every indication that they are not going to do it. There is every indication that the inducements-and there have been very tasty inducements-are going to fail. I believe that is another important consideration in dealing with the proposal for public ownership of the banking system of Canada.
As I said earlier there is a lot of mythology concerning the banking system, and one of the most persistent myths about the present banking system in Canada is that there is danger to the liquidity of the banks' assets.
I believe my leader pointed out this afternoon that in actual fact the proportion of quickly realizable assets in the banks' portfolios has increased tremendously in recent years. From that point of view there is no danger of the banks getting into difficulty through lack of liquidity of their assets.
There is another much more important consideration, and I suggest it is this. Every one of us knows that since the failure of the Home Bank no government in Canada could possibly allow any bank to fail. There is no possibility of it failing at all. The banks will be protected from that danger. As I say, the government has it in hand, and quite rightly, because it is essential that the financial system should be protected from every one of these dangers. I would suggest that the proper way to regard our banking system is as perhaps our most important public utility. Not so many years ago there were people who were quite sure we were on the high road to bolshevism when we so much as took over a lighting system and operated it municipally, but today we find on all sides those who are firm advocates of public ownership for the provision of essential public 
services. I suggest to you, sir, that there is no more essential public service than that of looking after the savings of the people, and of placing them in proper investments for the social welfare of the people.
Earlier this evening the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) had something to say about the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. I was very interested in his remarks because I happened to have with me the latest report of that bank. Before dealing with that, I might spend a moment or two discussing the history of that bank, because it has considerable interest to us as Canadians. This bank was established largely through the efforts of a Canadian, a rather famous character in Australian history, known as King O'Malley.

their job; they would be faithless to their trust if at all times they did not safeguard the interests of their shareholders. And when those interests come in conflict with the public interest, then if the directors are to be faithful to their trust they must abandon the public interest. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, you cannot marry publicly-controlled financial systems to a private profit motive, because the marriage just will not last.
My hon. friend from Peace River asked what greater public utility there could be than money and credit. I quite agree with him; there is no greater public utility than money and credit. But that has been the burden of the song of socialists all along with respect to the financial system, that it is the most important public utility and for that reason must be removed from private hands where, perforce, it must serve private interests before public interests. Just as today no one would suggest that our highway system should be returned to private ownership, where at one time it was controlled; just as ill people would insist that our highways should be kept open and operating at all times, and that they should not be endangered by floods or disaster of any kind, so should the highways of commerce, as represented by the banking system, be brought under public control for precisely the same reason.
I suggest to hon. members that, although today the vast majority of members in the House of Commons will, without thought, vote against the proposition put forward by this group, it will not be many years before even many of those members now sitting in the house will accept as a matter of course the principle that the banking system should be publicly owned.
Professor Giblin in his book has something to say with regard to the attitude of a very famous financier in Great Britain, Mr. Montagu Norman, who had considerable to do with the original work of setting up the Commonwealth Bank as a central bank. One of the things that gave Mr. Norman pause with regard to establishing a publicly-owned commonwealth bank as a central bank was the fact that it was publicly-owned. He is quoted in this book as saying that he was unable to see how a publicly-owned institution could possibly operate as a central bank. That happened not very many years ago; in fact it was only 30 years ago. At that time Mr. Montagu Norman was the voice of orthodox finance throughout the world; his word was gospel. Yet he was unable to see how a publicly-owned institution could function as a central bank.

Not long after that the Bank of Canada was established. The same idea that apparently had been in Mr. Norman's mind was still in the minds of those who established the Bank of Canada in its original form. The result was that it was set up as a curious hybrid, publicly-owned and privately-owned. But it was not very long before the logic of events decided what should be done with the Bank of Canada, and no one today would suggest it should be returned to private hands. No one, I think, would suggest it has not been possible for the publicly-owned institution, the Bank of Canada, to function effectively as the controlling agency of currency in the Dominion of Canada.
While I know hon. members will throw out the suggestion we have made, I hope the time is not far distant when many of them will accept as a matter of course the principle that this vital necessity in the heart of our society should be brought under public control. The major argument I have heard advanced against the scheme has always been that there might be political influence in connection with loans made by that institution. I asked the gentleman to whom I referred a short time ago that very question, when I was speaking about the Commonwealth Bank. He told me there had never been even the slightest suspicion in Australia that political influence had in any way affected the bank's lending habits or their attitude in granting loans, so I think we can dismiss that as being purely a chimera of the imagination. But I suggest that you had better keep on thinking about it; you had better marshal some facts as argument against it in the years to come, because 1 am quite sure you are going to need them to stem the tide of public opinion that is going to sweep us into a position of public ownership of the financial system of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to support the submission made by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Anderson) with regard to the amendment of section 88 of the bill we have before us. I am sure that many fruit and vegetable growers in the Niagara area will be grateful to the hon. member for Norfolk for bringing this matter to the attention of hon. members, first in 1951 when he introduced it as a private member's bill and again when speaking in this debate.
The hon. member for Norfolk has proposed that any reservation as to security under the provisions of section 88 should be eliminated. I suggest that some security should be given to the grower by creating a reservation under

the operations of section 88 of the bill. Under the provisions of section 88 a bank is permitted to take additional security by way of a warehouse receipt or a notice of intention under the provisions of the section. This document gives the bank precedence over all claims except those of wage earners as covered by the provisions of subsection 5.
I assume this protection has been given to the banks because of the fact that the possession of property raises a certain presumption of ownership by the possessor. Thus the bank is provided with ample security through knowing that their customers have in their hands a tangible product on which a loan can be made. It is quite satisfactory when considered from that side of the picture.
But on the other side of the picture we find that the fruit and vegetable growers and other primary producers have put forth hard work and sustained effort in the development of their products. There is altogether too little profit for the primary producer in the first place. The fruit and vegetable producer is required to deliver his produce to the canner. After strict scrutiny and examination the canner accepts the natural products which have been delivered to him. The grower has actually provided the raw material which is the essence of the business itself.
In the last four years three canners in our particular area have made assignments in bankruptcy. They were well stocked with natural products which had been processed by them. These assignments have brought about a resultant loss of over $1 million to the growers in the area. This loss is spread over the four counties of Wentworth, Haldi-mand, Welland and Lincoln. The loss is quite heavy, and these people who have been obliged to accept the burden cannot afford to bear it.
An individual may make an assignment in bankruptcy and then commence business again under his wife's name; as an incorporated company, or in the name of some other relative. The whole process is started over again. I think some protection must be given to the primary producer who produces the actual product. I appreciate the fact that a bank must look to a manufacturer for some security before it provides a line of credit, but the provision of this additional priority to the grower may cause the bank to exercise greater care before making a loan, and they might become a bit more selective as to the type of client or customer to whom a loan would be made.
I think the amendment suggested by the hon. member to delete the priority provision
The Bank Act
altogether probably would not be a safe thing to do. I do urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to give serious consideration to providing a priority similar to the one given by subsection 5 of section 88. This could be done by adding a subsection to provide that the products of the soil shall be given a similar priority when delivered to a processor.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DECENNIAL REVISION, EXTENSION OF CHARTERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the two main amendments to the Bank Act relate, first, to long-term loans being made under the National Housing Act and, second, to changes in the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks. In so far as the first of those is concerned, I think it is a debatable point. Many feel that it will be a mistake for the chartered banks to go into the field of long-term loans on real estate, but personally I believe it would permit them to perform a worth-while service by working under this formula.
The second amendment provides that the minimum cash reserve requirement be raised from 5 per cent to 8 per cent and be made variable upward to 12 per cent at the discretion of the Bank of Canada. As I pointed out when I spoke on the amendment to the Bank of Canada Act, this is definitely a step in the right direction, but we feel that the limit of 12 per cent is too restrictive, that it should be at least 16 per cent, and it might be well worth while to make it higher to meet future needs.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) pointed out that while the Bank of Canada can take steps to increase or decrease the cash reserve of the chartered banks, the final decision rests with the chartered banks as to whether or not they will make loans. I would say it is not really as simple as that. I would say that the final decision really rests with the government, because it all depends on the type of policy we have in operation as to whether or not chartered banks can expand their loans.
For instance, if you have a situation where our production is at a very high level, where inventories are accumulating, where unemployment is increasing, where industry is beginning to curtail production because it cannot sell its goods, it would be questionable whether it would be wise for the chartered banks to expand loans to industry which cannot sell its existing supplies of goods. We face that situation in a depression. So I would think that in that regard the decision rests not so much with the chartered banks but with the government adopting a type of policy which makes it possible for us to maintain production at a high level. If we create a condition where industry is able to expand production on a profitable

The Bank Act
to build houses, it will have to be a different type of action to achieve that objective. To try to do so by expanding taxation or by borrowing the savings of the people would certainly not increase the purchasing power of the people. On the other hand, the government may decide upon a policy of expanding the money supply by borrowing from the chartered banks.
At this point I want to examine briefly the financial machinery we have at our disposal, and the division of responsibility as among the chartered banks, the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance. When I refer to the chartered banks, I want to deal with them collectively, as one body. The chartered banks are responsible for making loans to industry; and of course loans can be reallocated as between industries on the basis of existing cash reserves. The expansion, of course, depends to a large extent upon the action the Bank of Canada may take. Hence action of the chartered banks in expanding or contracting loans will depend upon action of the Bank of Canada.
However, a situation such as we had in the 1930's or the situation that may well develop at the present time, if it continues to deteriorate, cannot be met by that means alone. Industry cannot expand without markets. If we are going to have an expansion of industry, we will first of all have to provide for expanding markets; and expanding markets, of course, depend upon maintaining an effective demand. Therefore
if we are going to bring about a situation where there can be an adequate supply of purchasing power, it will require action by the federal government in order to expand the purchasing power of the people either by capital projects, by social services or by reduction of taxation, or by a combination of all three.
I want to point out that it is quite evident that we cannot hope to expand the purchasing power of the people by obtaining money through an expansion of taxation, especially the sales tax or taxation of people in the lower income groups. Neither can we hope to expand the purchasing power of the people by expanding borrowings from their savings. Therefore, in a situation such as we had in the thirties, or a situation that may develop at the present time, it is necessary to have an expansion of credit and we insist that should be by using the Bank of Canada rather than the chartered banks.
Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Quelch the debate was adjourned.
